entry.sum: A Dedekind domain is a Noetherian, integrally closed integral domain in which every nonzero prime ideal is maximal; equivalently, a Noetherian domain whose localisations at nonzero primes are discrete valuation rings, or a domain in which every nonzero ideal factors uniquely into prime ideals. Rings of integers of number fields and coordinate rings of smooth affine curves are the basic examples. Their nonzero fractional ideals form a free abelian group on the primes, and the quotient by principal ideals, the class group, measures the failure of unique factorisation of elements.

entry.why: Dedekind domains are the setting of algebraic number theory: unique factorisation of ideals, the class group, the splitting of primes in extensions and class field theory are all statements about them, and the same theory describes the arithmetic of smooth algebraic curves.

links.note: The coordinate ring of a smooth irreducible affine curve over an algebraically closed field is a Dedekind domain; the factorisation of $(f)$ records the orders of vanishing of $f$, and the class group is the Picard group of the curve (for an elliptic curve minus its origin it is the group of points).

Baanen, Dahmen, Narayanan and Nuccio formalised Dedekind domains in Lean's Mathlib with three equivalent definitions, proved unique factorisation of ideals, and proved finiteness of class groups of global fields.

blocks.body:
In $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ the number $6$ has two essentially different factorisations into irreducible elements, $6 = 2\cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$. On [[ideals]] you saw the repair: as ideals,
$$(6) = P_2^2\,P_3\,P_3',$$
with $P_2 = (2, 1+\sqrt{-5})$, $P_3 = (3, 1+\sqrt{-5})$, $P_3' = (3, 1-\sqrt{-5})$, and the two factorisations of the number are two groupings of the same four prime ideals. That page stated Dedekind's theorem (every nonzero ideal of a ring of integers is uniquely a product of prime ideals) without proof.

This page proves it, and finds the exact class of rings where it holds. Kummer introduced "ideal numbers" in the 1840s to restore unique factorisation in cyclotomic integers; Dedekind replaced them by ideals, sets of actual numbers, in his supplements to Dirichlet's lectures (1871, 1877/79, 1894); Hilbert's Zahlbericht (1897) spread his approach; and Emmy Noether's axiomatic work (1921, 1927) singled out the abstract rings in which ideals factor uniquely. These are the Dedekind domains: Noetherian, integrally closed, with every nonzero prime ideal maximal. The first two families of examples are the rings of integers of number fields and the coordinate rings of smooth affine curves, which is why the notion sits between number theory and algebraic geometry.

The route through the page:

1. Discrete valuation rings: the local picture, where every ideal is a power of one prime.
2. Fractional ideals and invertibility: the tool that lets us divide by an ideal.
3. Dedekind domains: the definition, examples, non-examples, and why four different-looking definitions agree.
4. Unique factorisation of ideals, the valuations $v_{\mathfrak p}$, and "to contain is to divide".
5. The Chinese remainder theorem, approximation and two generators for every ideal.
6. The norm of an ideal.
7. The class group, which measures how far a Dedekind domain is from being a principal ideal domain.
8. Localising a Dedekind domain, and what happens to the class group.
9. Rings of integers: why integral closures of Dedekind domains in finite separable extensions are Dedekind.
10. Finitely generated modules over a Dedekind domain and the Steinitz class.

By the end you should be able to read the preliminaries of papers on class groups, factorisation, number fields and module lattices without being stopped by the ideal theory. How primes split in an extension (ramification indices, residue degrees, the Dedekind-Kummer theorem, decomposition groups) is a subject of its own and is only introduced here; finiteness of the class group of a number field is proved on [[class-group]].

blocks.title: Discrete valuation rings
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to recognise a discrete valuation ring, compute with its valuation, and prove that a Noetherian local domain is a discrete valuation ring as soon as its maximal ideal is principal.

Start with a question you can answer from [[localization]]. In $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, the rationals whose denominator is prime to $3$, which elements are units, and what are the ideals? Every nonzero $x \in \mathbb Q$ can be written $x = 3^k a/b$ with $3 \nmid ab$, and $x \in \mathbb Z_{(3)}$ exactly when $k \ge 0$. So $x = 3^k u$ with $u$ a unit, and an ideal is determined by the smallest exponent $k$ it contains: the nonzero ideals are $3^k\mathbb Z_{(3)}$. All of the divisibility in this ring is recorded by one integer, the exponent of $3$. Rings with this property are the local building blocks of Dedekind domains. We follow Aitken's systematic account, which starts from the valuation; the Stacks Project and Sutherland use the same notion.

blocks.title: Discrete valuation ring
blocks.body:
Let $K$ be a field. A discrete valuation on $K$ is a surjective map $v\colon K^\times \to \mathbb Z$ such that for all $x, y \in K^\times$
$$v(xy) = v(x) + v(y), \qquad v(x + y) \ge \min(v(x), v(y)) \ \text{ if } x + y \ne 0.$$
One puts $v(0) = +\infty$, so that both rules hold for all $x, y \in K$. The set
$$\mathcal O_v = \{x \in K : v(x) \ge 0\}$$
is the valuation ring of $v$. A discrete valuation ring (DVR) is a ring of the form $\mathcal O_v$ for some discrete valuation $v$ on its fraction field. An element $\pi$ with $v(\pi) = 1$ is a uniformiser.

The standard example is the $p$-adic valuation $v_p$ on $\mathbb Q$ (see [[p-adic-valuation]]), with valuation ring $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ and uniformiser $p$. For a field $k$, the order of vanishing at $a \in k$ is a discrete valuation on $k(x)$ whose valuation ring is $k[x]_{(x - a)}$, with uniformiser $x - a$.

blocks.title: Structure of a discrete valuation ring
blocks.body:
Let $R = \mathcal O_v$ be a DVR with fraction field $K$ and uniformiser $\pi$. Then:

1. $v(1) = v(-1) = 0$, and $v(x + y) = \min(v(x), v(y))$ whenever $v(x) \ne v(y)$.
2. $R$ is a local domain; its units are the elements with $v(x) = 0$ and its maximal ideal is $\mathfrak m = \{v > 0\} = \pi R$.
3. Every $x \in K^\times$ can be written uniquely as $x = u\pi^k$ with $u \in R^\times$ and $k \in \mathbb Z$; necessarily $k = v(x)$.
4. The nonzero ideals of $R$ are exactly the $\pi^k R$ with $k \ge 0$, and they are distinct. So $R$ is a principal ideal domain with exactly one nonzero prime ideal, it is Noetherian, and $\dim R = 1$.
5. $R$ is integrally closed in $K$.

1. $v(1) = v(1 \cdot 1) = 2v(1)$ gives $v(1) = 0$, and $2v(-1) = v(1) = 0$ gives $v(-1) = 0$, so $v(-y) = v(y)$. If $v(x) < v(y)$, then $v(x) = v((x + y) + (-y))$, which is $\ge \min(v(x + y), v(y))$; the minimum cannot be $v(y) > v(x)$, so it is $v(x + y)$ and $v(x + y) \le v(x)$. Together with $v(x + y) \ge \min(v(x), v(y)) = v(x)$ this gives equality.

2. $R$ contains $0, \pm 1$ and is closed under sums and products by the two rules, so it is a subring of $K$, hence a domain. For $x \in R \setminus \{0\}$, the inverse $x^{-1} \in K$ has $v(x^{-1}) = -v(x)$, so $x$ is a unit of $R$ iff $v(x) = 0$. The non-units of $R$ are therefore the elements with $v > 0$; they form an ideal (closed under addition by the second rule, under multiplication by $R$ by the first). A ring whose non-units form an ideal is local, by the characterisation on [[local-rings]], and that ideal is the maximal ideal. If $x \in \mathfrak m$ then $v(x\pi^{-1}) = v(x) - 1 \ge 0$, so $x = \pi\cdot x\pi^{-1} \in \pi R$; hence $\mathfrak m = \pi R$.

3. Put $k = v(x)$ and $u = x\pi^{-k}$. Then $v(u) = 0$, so $u$ is a unit and $x = u\pi^k$. If $u\pi^k = u'\pi^l$, applying $v$ gives $k = l$, and then $u = u'$.

4. Let $I \ne 0$ be an ideal and $k$ the smallest value of $v$ on $I \setminus \{0\}$ (values are integers $\ge 0$). Take $x \in I$ with $v(x) = k$, so $x = u\pi^k$ and $\pi^k = u^{-1}x \in I$; hence $\pi^kR \subseteq I$. Conversely every $y \in I$ has $v(y) \ge k$, so $y = \pi^k \cdot y\pi^{-k}$ with $y\pi^{-k} \in R$. Thus $I = \pi^kR$, and $k$ is recovered from $I$ as its minimal valuation, so the ideals are distinct. The ideal $\pi^kR$ is prime only for $k = 1$ (for $k \ge 2$, $\pi \cdot \pi^{k-1} \in \pi^kR$ with neither factor in it; for $k = 0$ it is $R$). So the primes are $0$ and $\pi R$, and $\dim R = 1$; a PID is Noetherian.

5. Let $x \in K$ satisfy $x^n + a_1x^{n-1} + \dots + a_n = 0$ with $a_i \in R$, and suppose $x \notin R$, so $v(x) < 0$. Each term $a_ix^{n-i}$ ($i \ge 1$) has valuation $v(a_i) + (n-i)v(x) \ge (n - i)v(x) > nv(x)$. So by part 1 (applied repeatedly) the sum $a_1x^{n-1} + \dots + a_n$ has valuation $> nv(x) = v(x^n)$, or is $0$. But it equals $-x^n$, which has valuation exactly $nv(x)$. Contradiction; so $x \in R$.

blocks.title: When is a local ring a DVR?

blocks.body:
The Stacks Project lists these conditions in its Lemma 10.119.7. We prove (1) implies (2) and (3), then (2) implies (1) following Aitken's Theorem 11; the implication from (3) to (2) needs the invertibility theorem and is proved in the section on Dedekind domains below.

(1) implies (2) and (3): this is parts 2, 4 and 5 of the structure theorem.

(2) implies (1). Let $\mathfrak m = \pi R$; $\pi \ne 0$ because $R$ is not a field.

Step 1: dividing by $\pi$ strictly enlarges principal ideals. If $0 \ne x = x_1\pi$, then $xR \subsetneq x_1R$. Indeed if $xR = x_1R$ then $x_1 = xy$ for some $y$, so $x = xy\pi$, $x(1 - y\pi) = 0$; but $1 - y\pi$ is a unit (it is not in $\mathfrak m$), so $x = 0$.

Step 2: every nonzero $x$ is $u\pi^k$. If $x$ is a unit take $k = 0$. Otherwise $x \in \mathfrak m$, so $x = x_1\pi$; if $x_1$ is not a unit, $x_1 = x_2\pi$, and so on. If this never stopped, step 1 would give a strictly increasing chain $xR \subsetneq x_1R \subsetneq x_2R \subsetneq \cdots$, impossible in a Noetherian ring. So some $x_k$ is a unit $u$ and $x = u\pi^k$.

Step 3: uniqueness. If $u\pi^k = u'\pi^l$ with $k < l$, cancelling $\pi^k$ (we are in a domain) gives $u = u'\pi^{l-k} \in \mathfrak m$, which is not a unit. So $k = l$ and $u = u'$.

Step 4: the valuation. Define $v(u\pi^k) = k$ on $R \setminus \{0\}$. Clearly $v(xy) = v(x) + v(y)$. If $x = u\pi^k$, $y = u'\pi^l$ with $k \le l$ and $x + y \ne 0$, then $x + y = \pi^k(u + u'\pi^{l-k})$ and the bracket lies in $R$, so $v(x + y) \ge k$. Extend to $K$ by $v(a/b) = v(a) - v(b)$; this is well defined because $a/b = a'/b'$ means $ab' = a'b$, so $v(a) + v(b') = v(a') + v(b)$. It is surjective ($v(\pi^k) = k$) and satisfies both rules. Finally $\mathcal O_v = R$: elements of $R$ have $v \ge 0$, and if $v(a/b) \ge 0$ with $a = u\pi^k$, $b = u'\pi^l$, then $k \ge l$ and $a/b = uu'^{-1}\pi^{k-l} \in R$.

blocks.title: What is a discrete valuation ring?

items.label: A valuation
items.body: The ring of elements of nonnegative valuation for a surjective $v\colon K^\times \to \mathbb Z$ with $v(xy) = v(x) + v(y)$ and $v(x + y) \ge \min$. This is Aitken's definition (Definitions 2-3), and it is the one that makes computations with orders of zeros and exponents of primes transparent.

items.label: A local PID
items.body: A principal ideal domain with exactly one nonzero prime ideal (Aitken, Corollary 12). Sutherland identifies $k[x]_{(x-a)}$ and $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ as DVRs this way (Examples 2.4-2.5): local, principal, not a field.

items.label: Principal maximal ideal
items.body: A Noetherian local domain whose maximal ideal is generated by one nonzero element (Stacks Lemma 10.119.7(4); Aitken, Theorem 11). This is the criterion one checks in practice, as in the example of $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]_{P_2}$ below.

items.label: Regular or normal of dimension one
items.body: A regular local ring of dimension $1$, or a Noetherian local normal (integrally closed) domain of dimension $1$ (Stacks Lemma 10.119.7(3) and (5)). Gathmann's definition of Dedekind domains uses the regular version (Definition 13.1); Sutherland's proof that Dedekind domains are locally DVRs uses the normal version.

blocks.title: A non-principal prime becomes principal locally
blocks.body: In $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ let $P_2 = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$, the prime with $P_2^2 = (2)$ from [[ideals]]; recall $P_2 = \{a + b\sqrt{-5} : a \equiv b \pmod 2\}$. Show that $P_2D_{P_2}$ is generated by $1 + \sqrt{-5}$, so that $D_{P_2}$ is a DVR with uniformiser $1 + \sqrt{-5}$, although $P_2$ is not principal in $D$. Compute the valuations of $2$, $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ and $1 - \sqrt{-5}$.
blocks.solution:
In $D_{P_2}$ every element of $D \setminus P_2$ is a unit. The element $3 = 3 + 0\sqrt{-5}$ has $3 \not\equiv 0 \pmod 2$, so $3 \notin P_2$ and $3$ is a unit. Now $(1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5}) = 1 + 5 = 6$, so
$$2 = \frac{(1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5})}{3} \in (1 + \sqrt{-5})D_{P_2}.$$
Hence $P_2D_{P_2} = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})D_{P_2} = (1 + \sqrt{-5})D_{P_2}$: the maximal ideal of the local ring $D_{P_2}$ is principal. $D_{P_2}$ is a Noetherian local domain (a localisation of the Noetherian domain $D$), not a field, so by the theorem just proved it is a DVR with uniformiser $\pi = 1 + \sqrt{-5}$.

Valuations: $v(1 + \sqrt{-5}) = 1$. Next,
$$\frac{1 - \sqrt{-5}}{1 + \sqrt{-5}} = \frac{(1 - \sqrt{-5})^2}{6} = \frac{-4 - 2\sqrt{-5}}{6} = -\frac{2 + \sqrt{-5}}{3},$$
and neither $2 + \sqrt{-5}$ nor $3$ lies in $P_2$ (in both, $a \not\equiv b \pmod 2$), so this quotient is a unit and $v(1 - \sqrt{-5}) = 1$. Finally $v(2) = v(1 + \sqrt{-5}) + v(1 - \sqrt{-5}) - v(3) = 1 + 1 - 0 = 2$, matching $(2) = P_2^2$. Locally at $P_2$ the failure of unique factorisation is invisible: there is only one prime, $1 + \sqrt{-5}$, up to units, and $2$ is its square times a unit.

items.q: Is $\mathbb Z_{(2)} \cap \mathbb Z_{(3)}$ (inside $\mathbb Q$) a DVR?
items.a: No: it has two maximal ideals, generated by $2$ and by $3$, so it is not local.

items.q: What is $v_5(50/3)$, and is $50/3 \in \mathbb Z_{(5)}$?
items.a: $50/3 = 5^2 \cdot 2/3$, so $v_5 = 2 \ge 0$ and yes, it lies in $\mathbb Z_{(5)}$ (it is $25$ times a unit).

items.q: Name two different uniformisers of $k[x]_{(x)}$.
items.a: Any element of valuation $1$, for instance $x$ and $x + x^2 = x(1 + x)$, since $1 + x$ is a unit there.

items.q: Can a field be a DVR?
items.a: No. A discrete valuation is surjective onto $\mathbb Z$, so some $\pi$ has $v(\pi) = 1$ and is a non-unit of $\mathcal O_v$; a field has no nonzero non-units.

items.q: Write $45/14$ and $7/27$ in the form $3^k u$ with $u$ a unit of $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$. Which of them lie in $\mathbb Z_{(3)}$?
items.hint: Factor out the power of $3$ from numerator and denominator.
items.solution: $45/14 = 3^2 \cdot 5/14$ with $5/14$ a unit (numerator and denominator prime to $3$), so $v_3 = 2$ and $45/14 \in \mathbb Z_{(3)}$, indeed in $9\mathbb Z_{(3)}$. $7/27 = 3^{-3}\cdot 7$, so $v_3 = -3 < 0$ and $7/27 \notin \mathbb Z_{(3)}$.

items.q: Let $R$ be a DVR with uniformiser $\pi$ and $n \ge 1$. Show that $R/\pi^nR$ has exactly $n + 1$ ideals, and that it is a local ring in which every ideal is principal.
items.hint: Ideals of a quotient $R/I$ correspond to ideals of $R$ containing $I$.
items.solution: Ideals of $R/\pi^nR$ correspond to ideals $J \supseteq \pi^nR$ of $R$. By the structure theorem $J = \pi^kR$ for some $k \ge 0$ (or $J = 0$, which does not contain $\pi^n R$), and $\pi^kR \supseteq \pi^nR$ iff $k \le n$ (compare minimal valuations). So the ideals are $\pi^kR/\pi^nR$ for $k = 0, 1, \dots, n$: exactly $n + 1$ of them, each generated by the image of $\pi^k$. The only maximal one is $\pi R/\pi^nR$, so the ring is local.

items.q: Show that the only local ring $R$ with $\mathbb Z \subseteq R \subseteq \mathbb Q$ whose maximal ideal contains the prime $p$ is $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$.
items.hint: First show every integer prime to $p$ is a unit of $R$. Then show $1/p \notin R$ and use a B\'ezout relation.
items.solution: Let $\mathfrak m$ be the maximal ideal of $R$. Then $\mathfrak m \cap \mathbb Z$ is a prime ideal of $\mathbb Z$ containing $p$, so it equals $p\mathbb Z$. An integer $n$ prime to $p$ is not in $\mathfrak m$, hence is a unit of $R$ (in a local ring, everything outside $\mathfrak m$ is a unit); so $\mathbb Z_{(p)} \subseteq R$. Conversely let $a/b \in R$ in lowest terms and suppose $p \mid b$. Since $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ there are integers $s, t$ with $sa + tb = 1$, so $1/b = s(a/b) + t \in R$, and then $1/p = (b/p)\cdot(1/b) \in R$. But $p \in \mathfrak m$ is not a unit of $R$. Contradiction; so $p \nmid b$ and $a/b \in \mathbb Z_{(p)}$.

items.q: Let $k$ be a field and $R = k[x, y]_{(x, y)}$. Show that $R$ is not a DVR.
items.hint: If the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ were $\pi R$, then $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ would be at most one-dimensional over $k$.
items.solution: The maximal ideal is $\mathfrak m = (x, y)R$ and $R/\mathfrak m \cong k$ (evaluation at the origin). The images of $x$ and $y$ in $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ are linearly independent over $k$: if $\lambda x + \mu y \in \mathfrak m^2$ with $\lambda, \mu \in k$, then clearing denominators (an element $s \notin (x,y)$) gives $s(\lambda x + \mu y) \in (x, y)^2 k[x,y]$, and comparing linear terms, using $s(0,0) \ne 0$, forces $\lambda = \mu = 0$. So $\dim_k \mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2 \ge 2$. If $\mathfrak m = \pi R$, then $\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2$ would be spanned by the image of $\pi$, of dimension $\le 1$. So $\mathfrak m$ is not principal and $R$ is not a DVR (by the theorem, or directly since a DVR has principal maximal ideal). Alternatively: $R$ has the chain of primes $0 \subsetneq (x) \subsetneq (x, y)$, so $\dim R \ge 2$.

items.q: Let $R$ be a DVR with fraction field $K$. Show that the only rings $S$ with $R \subseteq S \subseteq K$ are $R$ and $K$.
items.hint: If $S$ contains an element of negative valuation, show $\pi^{-1} \in S$.
items.solution: Suppose $S \ne R$ and pick $x \in S \setminus R$, so $v(x) = -k$ with $k \ge 1$ and $x = u\pi^{-k}$ with $u \in R^\times$. Then $\pi^{-k} = u^{-1}x \in S$, and $\pi^{-1} = \pi^{k-1}\pi^{-k} \in S$. Every element of $K^\times$ is $u'\pi^m$ with $u' \in R^\times$, $m \in \mathbb Z$; if $m < 0$ it equals $u'(\pi^{-1})^{-m} \in S$, and if $m \ge 0$ it lies in $R \subseteq S$. So $S = K$. (Aitken, Proposition 20: a DVR is a maximal proper subring of its fraction field.)

blocks.body:
- A DVR is $\{x : v(x) \ge 0\}$ for a discrete valuation $v\colon K^\times \to \mathbb Z$; every $x \ne 0$ is $u\pi^{v(x)}$.
- Its nonzero ideals are $\pi^kR$, so it is a local PID with one nonzero prime, integrally closed, of dimension $1$.
- $v(x + y) = \min(v(x), v(y))$ when the two valuations differ.
- A Noetherian local domain (not a field) is a DVR iff its maximal ideal is principal iff it is integrally closed of dimension $1$.
- Example: $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]_{P_2}$ is a DVR with uniformiser $1 + \sqrt{-5}$, although $P_2$ is not principal.

blocks.title: Fractional ideals and invertibility
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to compute the colon $(A : I)$ of an ideal, decide whether an ideal is invertible, and check invertibility one maximal ideal at a time.

Why we need it: in $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ we have $P_3P_3' = (3)$, so
$$P_3 \cdot \tfrac13 P_3' = D.$$
The set $\tfrac13P_3'$ behaves like an inverse of $P_3$, but it is not an ideal of $D$: it contains $\tfrac13(1 - \sqrt{-5})$, which is not in $D$. To divide by ideals we must allow such $D$-submodules of the fraction field. Throughout, $A$ is a domain with fraction field $K$; recall from [[localization]] that we can regard every localisation $A_{\mathfrak p}$ as a subring of $K$. We follow Sutherland's Lectures 2 and 3, with Conrad's handout and Aitken for the general (not necessarily Noetherian) definitions.

blocks.title: Fractional ideals, the colon, invertible ideals
blocks.body:
A fractional ideal of $A$ is a nonzero $A$-submodule $I \subseteq K$ such that $dI \subseteq A$ for some nonzero $d \in A$ (a common denominator). The nonzero ideals of $A$ are the fractional ideals contained in $A$; to stress this one calls them integral ideals. For $x \in K^\times$ the principal fractional ideal is $(x) = xA$.

For fractional ideals $I, J$ the sum $I + J$ and product $IJ$ (finite sums $\sum x_iy_i$) are defined as for ideals, and
$$(I : J) = \{x \in K : xJ \subseteq I\}.$$
The fractional ideal $I$ is invertible if $IJ = A$ for some fractional ideal $J$. One writes $I^{-1}$ for $(A : I)$; it is the inverse when $I$ is invertible, but it is defined for every $I$.

For Noetherian $A$, Sutherland instead defines a fractional ideal as a nonzero finitely generated $A$-submodule of $K$; part 2 of the next theorem shows that the two definitions agree in that case.

blocks.title: Basic properties of fractional ideals
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a domain with fraction field $K$, and $I, J$ fractional ideals.

1. $I + J$, $IJ$, $I \cap J$ and $(A : I)$ are fractional ideals.
2. If $A$ is Noetherian, a nonzero $A$-submodule $I \subseteq K$ is a fractional ideal iff it is finitely generated.
3. $I$ is invertible iff $I\,(A : I) = A$. The inverse is then unique and equals $(A : I)$.
4. An invertible fractional ideal is finitely generated.
5. If $A$ is local, a fractional ideal is invertible iff it is principal.
6. If $A$ is Noetherian, then $I$ is invertible iff $I_{\mathfrak m} = IA_{\mathfrak m}$ is an invertible fractional ideal of $A_{\mathfrak m}$ for every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, iff every $I_{\mathfrak m}$ is principal.

Let $d, d'$ be common denominators of $I$ and $J$.

1. $dd'(I + J) \subseteq A$ and $dd'IJ \subseteq A$, and both are nonzero. For $I \cap J$: pick nonzero $x \in I$, $y \in J$; then $dx, d'y \in A$ and $z = (dx)(d'y)$ is nonzero, lies in $I$ (it is $(dd'y)x$ with $dd'y \in A$) and in $J$ (it is $(dd'x) y$). So $I \cap J \ne 0$, and $d$ is a common denominator. For $(A : I)$: it is an $A$-submodule; $d \in (A : I)$, so it is nonzero; and if $a = dx \ne 0$ is an element of $I \cap A$, then $a(A : I) \subseteq A$.

2. (Sutherland, Lemma 2.14.) If $I$ is generated by $r_1/s_1, \dots, r_n/s_n$, then $s_1\cdots s_n$ is a common denominator. Conversely if $dI \subseteq A$, then $dI$ is an ideal of $A$, generated by some $a_1, \dots, a_m$ because $A$ is Noetherian, and then $a_1/d, \dots, a_m/d$ generate $I$.

3. (Sutherland, Lemma 2.20.) If $IJ = A$ then $J \subseteq (A : I)$, so $A = IJ \subseteq I(A : I) \subseteq A$, where the last inclusion is the definition of the colon. Conversely, if $I(A : I) = A$ take $J = (A : I)$. Uniqueness: if $IJ = IJ' = A$ then $J = J(IJ') = (JI)J' = J'$.

4. Write $1 = \sum_{i=1}^n a_ib_i$ with $a_i \in I$ and $b_i \in (A : I)$. For $x \in I$, $x = \sum (xb_i)\,a_i$ with $xb_i \in A$; so $a_1, \dots, a_n$ generate $I$.

5. (Sutherland, Lemma 3.4.) A principal $(x)$ has inverse $(x^{-1})$. Conversely let $I(A : I) = A$ and write $1 = \sum a_ib_i$ as in part 4. Each $a_ib_i \in A$. If all of them lay in the maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, so would their sum $1$; so some $a_1b_1$ is a unit. For $x \in I$, $b_1x \in A$, and $x = (a_1b_1)^{-1}a_1(b_1x) \in a_1A$. Hence $I = (a_1)$.

6. (Sutherland, Theorem 3.2.) First, localisation commutes with products and with colons of finitely generated fractional ideals: $(IJ)_{\mathfrak m} = I_{\mathfrak m}J_{\mathfrak m}$ is clear, and if $I = (g_1, \dots, g_n)$ then $(A : I)_{\mathfrak m} = (A_{\mathfrak m} : I_{\mathfrak m})$. For the latter, "$\subseteq$" is clear; if $y \in K$ has $yg_i \in A_{\mathfrak m}$ for all $i$, write $yg_i = c_i/s_i$ with $s_i \notin \mathfrak m$ and put $s = s_1\cdots s_n$; then $sy \in (A : I)$ and $y = sy/s \in (A : I)_{\mathfrak m}$. Now $J = I(A : I)$ is an ideal of $A$, and $J = A$ iff $J$ lies in no maximal ideal iff $J_{\mathfrak m} = A_{\mathfrak m}$ for all $\mathfrak m$ (an ideal $J$ has $J_{\mathfrak m} = A_{\mathfrak m}$ exactly when $J \not\subseteq \mathfrak m$, by [[localization]]). Since $J_{\mathfrak m} = I_{\mathfrak m}(A_{\mathfrak m} : I_{\mathfrak m})$, this says: $I$ is invertible iff every $I_{\mathfrak m}$ is invertible (by part 3 over $A_{\mathfrak m}$; $I$ is finitely generated by part 2). The last equivalence is part 5 applied to the local rings $A_{\mathfrak m}$.

items.label: Has an inverse
items.body: $IJ = A$ for some fractional ideal $J$, equivalently $I\,(A : I) = A$ (Sutherland, Definition 2.19 and Lemma 2.20; Conrad §2). This is the form used to compute.

items.label: Locally principal
items.body: For Noetherian $A$: finitely generated and principal at every maximal ideal (Sutherland, Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.5; Aitken, Corollary 68). Invertibility is a local property, and locally it means principal.

items.label: Line bundle
items.body: An ideal $I$ with $IJ = (f)$ for a nonzerodivisor $f$ is a finitely generated, locally free module of rank $1$ (Stacks Lemma 10.120.16); conversely such modules are projective of rank one. In geometric language invertible ideals are line bundles, and the class group is the Picard group.

rows.text: For Noetherian $A$: a nonzero finitely generated $A$-submodule of $K$ (Definition 2.13); he notes the common-denominator definition for general $A$ (Remark 2.15). He writes $I \div J$ for the colon.
A nonzero $A$-submodule $I \subseteq K$ with $dI \subseteq A$ for some nonzero $d \in A$; Gathmann writes $R :_K I$ for the colon.
Fractional ideals may be zero, with the convention $0^{-1} = 0$; most texts require them to be nonzero.

blocks.title: The inverse of the prime above 2 in Z[√−5]
blocks.body: Let $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ and $P_2 = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$. Compute $(D : P_2)$ directly from the definition, and check that $P_2$ is invertible.
blocks.solution:
Write $x = u + v\sqrt{-5}$ with $u, v \in \mathbb Q$. Since $P_2$ is generated by $2$ and $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ as a $D$-module, $x \in (D : P_2)$ iff $2x \in D$ and $x(1 + \sqrt{-5}) \in D$.

From $2x \in D$: $2u, 2v \in \mathbb Z$, so $x = (a + b\sqrt{-5})/2$ with $a, b \in \mathbb Z$.

Then
$$x(1 + \sqrt{-5}) = \frac{(a - 5b) + (a + b)\sqrt{-5}}{2},$$
which lies in $D$ iff $a - 5b$ and $a + b$ are even, i.e. iff $a \equiv b \pmod 2$ (the two conditions agree since $a - 5b = (a + b) - 6b$).

So $(D : P_2) = \{(a + b\sqrt{-5})/2 : a \equiv b \pmod 2\} = \tfrac12 P_2$, using $P_2 = \{a + b\sqrt{-5} : a \equiv b \pmod 2\}$. Therefore
$$P_2\,(D : P_2) = \tfrac12 P_2^2 = \tfrac12 (2) = D,$$
using $P_2^2 = (2)$ from [[ideals]]. So $P_2$ is invertible with $P_2^{-1} = \tfrac12P_2$, although it is not principal: by part 5 this is only possible because $D$ is not local, and indeed $P_2$ becomes principal in $D_{P_2}$ (previous section).

blocks.title: Two ideals that are not invertible
blocks.body:
(a) Let $A = \mathbb Z + 2i\mathbb Z \subseteq \mathbb Z[i]$, the set of $a + bi$ with $a \in \mathbb Z$, $b \in 2\mathbb Z$, and $I = 2\mathbb Z[i]$. Show that $I$ is an ideal of $A$, compute $(A : I)$, and show that $I$ is not invertible.

(b) Let $k$ be a field, $A = k[x, y]$ and $I = (x, y)$. Show that $(A : I) = A$, so $I$ is not invertible.
blocks.solution:
(a) $I = \{2m + 2ni\}$ lies in $A$ and is closed under multiplication by $A$ (even by $\mathbb Z[i]$), so it is an ideal of $A$. As a $\mathbb Z$-module $I$ is spanned by $2$ and $2i$, so for $x = p + qi$ ($p, q \in \mathbb Q$), $x \in (A : I)$ iff $2x \in A$ and $2ix \in A$: every element of $I$ is $2m + 2ni$, and $x(2m + 2ni) = m(2x) + n(2ix)$. Now $2x = 2p + 2qi \in A$ requires $2p \in \mathbb Z$ and $2q \in 2\mathbb Z$, so $q \in \mathbb Z$; and $2ix = -2q + 2pi \in A$ requires $2p \in 2\mathbb Z$, so $p \in \mathbb Z$. Conversely if $x \in \mathbb Z[i]$ then $xI \subseteq 2\mathbb Z[i] \subseteq A$. So $(A : I) = \mathbb Z[i]$ and
$$I\,(A : I) = 2\mathbb Z[i]\cdot\mathbb Z[i] = 2\mathbb Z[i] \ne A,$$
since $1 \notin 2\mathbb Z[i]$. By part 3, $I$ is not invertible (Sutherland, Example 2.21). Note $A/I \cong \mathbb Z/2$ (the class of $a + bi$ is $a \bmod 2$), so $I$ is a maximal ideal of $A$: a non-invertible prime.

(b) Let $f \in (A : I)$; write $f = p/q$ with $p, q \in A$ coprime ($A$ is a UFD, see [[ufds]]). Then $xf, yf \in A$, so $q \mid xp$ and $q \mid yp$, and since $\gcd(p, q) = 1$, $q \mid x$ and $q \mid y$. So $q$ is a unit and $f \in A$. Thus $(A : I) = A$ and $I(A : I) = I \ne A$ (Baanen et al. §5.2; Gathmann Example 13.21).

blocks.body:
- $I^{-1} = (A : I)$ is always defined, and the notation suggests an inverse, but $I\,I^{-1} = A$ holds only when $I$ is invertible. In both non-examples above $I\,(A : I) = I$.
- A fractional ideal need not lie in $A$, and an $A$-submodule of $K$ need not be a fractional ideal: $\mathbb Z_{(2)}$ and $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ are $\mathbb Z$-submodules of $\mathbb Q$ with no common denominator (Gathmann, Example 13.16).
- Invertible does not mean principal. Principal fractional ideals are invertible, but $P_2 \subseteq \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is invertible and not principal. It is only over local rings that the two notions agree.

items.q: Is $\mathbb Z[1/2]$ a fractional ideal of $\mathbb Z$?
items.a: No. It has no common denominator ($d\,\mathbb Z[1/2] \not\subseteq \mathbb Z$ for every $d \ne 0$), equivalently it is not finitely generated.

items.q: If $I$ is invertible and $IJ = IJ'$, must $J = J'$?
items.a: Yes: multiply both sides by $I^{-1}$.

items.q: Let $A$ be a local domain and $I = (a, b)$ an invertible ideal. What can you say?
items.a: $I$ is principal, and in fact generated by $a$ or by $b$: in the proof of part 5 one of the products $a_ib_i$ is a unit, and the corresponding $a_i$ generates.

items.q: Is the product of two invertible fractional ideals invertible? Is the sum?
items.a: The product is, with inverse $I^{-1}J^{-1}$. The sum need not be: in $k[x, y]$, $(x) + (y) = (x, y)$ is not invertible although $(x)$ and $(y)$ are.

items.q: In $\mathbb Z$, show that $I = \tfrac23\mathbb Z + \tfrac56\mathbb Z$ is principal, find a generator, and find $(\mathbb Z : I)$.
items.hint: Put everything over the denominator $6$.
items.solution: $I = \tfrac16(4\mathbb Z + 5\mathbb Z) = \tfrac16\gcd(4, 5)\mathbb Z = \tfrac16\mathbb Z$. So $I = (1/6)$ and $(\mathbb Z : I) = 6\mathbb Z$, with $I \cdot 6\mathbb Z = \mathbb Z$.

items.q: Show that a product $IJ$ of fractional ideals is invertible if and only if both $I$ and $J$ are.
items.hint: If $L$ is an inverse of $IJ$, what is $I \cdot (JL)$?
items.solution: If $I, J$ are invertible then $(IJ)(I^{-1}J^{-1}) = A$. Conversely if $(IJ)L = A$, then $I(JL) = A$ and $J(IL) = A$, and $JL$, $IL$ are fractional ideals (part 1), so $I$ and $J$ are invertible.

items.q: Let $A = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ and $P = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-3})$. Show that $P$ is the set of $a + b\sqrt{-3}$ with $a \equiv b \pmod 2$, compute $(A : P)$, and show $P(A : P) = P$. Which element of $(A : P)$ is integral over $A$ but not in $A$?
items.hint: Imitate the computation of $(D : P_2)$ in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$; also compute $P^2$.
items.solution:
The map $a + b\sqrt{-3} \mapsto a - b \bmod 2$ is a ring homomorphism $A \to \mathbb Z/2$ (it sends $\sqrt{-3}$ to $1$, and $1^2 \equiv -3 \pmod 2$); its kernel contains $2$ and $1 + \sqrt{-3}$, and conversely $a + b\sqrt{-3} = b(1 + \sqrt{-3}) + (a - b)$ lies in $P$ when $a - b$ is even. So $P$ is that kernel, a maximal ideal of index $2$.

$(A : P)$: as before $x = (a + b\sqrt{-3})/2$ with $a, b \in \mathbb Z$ (from $2x \in A$), and $x(1 + \sqrt{-3})$, which equals $\tfrac12\bigl((a - 3b) + (a + b)\sqrt{-3}\bigr)$, lies in $A$ iff $a \equiv b \pmod 2$. So $(A : P) = \tfrac12P$.

$P^2 = (4, 2(1 + \sqrt{-3}), (1 + \sqrt{-3})^2)$ and $(1 + \sqrt{-3})^2 = -2 + 2\sqrt{-3} = 2(-1 + \sqrt{-3})$ with $-1 + \sqrt{-3} \in P$. All generators lie in $2P$, and $2P = (4, 2 + 2\sqrt{-3}) \subseteq P^2$. So $P^2 = 2P$ and $P(A : P) = \tfrac12P^2 = P \ne A$. So $P$ is not invertible.

The element $\theta = (1 + \sqrt{-3})/2 \in \tfrac12 P$ satisfies $\theta^2 - \theta + 1 = 0$, so it is integral over $\mathbb Z$, hence over $A$, but $\theta \notin A$. This is exactly the element that the invertibility proof in the next section would produce, and it shows that $A$ is not integrally closed.

items.q: Show that the ideal $I = (2, x)$ of $\mathbb Z[x]$ is not invertible.
items.hint: Use that $\mathbb Z[x]$ is a UFD, as in the example of $(x, y) \subseteq k[x, y]$.
items.solution: Let $f = p/q \in (\mathbb Z[x] : I)$ with $p, q$ coprime in the UFD $\mathbb Z[x]$. From $2f, xf \in \mathbb Z[x]$ we get $q \mid 2p$ and $q \mid xp$, so $q \mid 2$ and $q \mid x$, so $q = \pm 1$. Hence $(\mathbb Z[x] : I) = \mathbb Z[x]$ and $I(\mathbb Z[x] : I) = I \ne \mathbb Z[x]$ (since $1 \notin (2, x)$: every element of $(2, x)$ has even constant term).

items.q: Let $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$. Show directly that $P_2$ is locally principal: for each maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ of $D$, find a generator of $P_2D_{\mathfrak m}$. Deduce again from part 6 that $P_2$ is invertible.
items.hint: Which maximal ideals contain $2$? Use $P_2^2 = (2)$.
items.solution:
If $\mathfrak m \supseteq P_2$ then $\mathfrak m = P_2$ ($P_2$ is maximal), and $P_2D_{P_2} = (1 + \sqrt{-5})D_{P_2}$ by the example in the previous section. If $\mathfrak m

otin \mathfrak m$: otherwise $P_2^2 = (2) \subseteq \mathfrak m$ and, $\mathfrak m$ being prime, $P_2 \subseteq \mathfrak m$.) So $P_2$ is locally principal, hence invertible by part 6, in agreement with $P_2^{-1} = 	frac12 P_2$.

blocks.title: Dedekind domains: definition, examples, and four equivalent definitions
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to decide whether a given ring is a Dedekind domain, using whichever of several equivalent definitions is easiest to check, and you will know the standard examples and counterexamples.

A question to keep in mind: what do $\mathbb Z$, $k[x]$, $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ and $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ have in common that $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$, $\mathbb Z + 2i\mathbb Z$ and $k[x, y]$ lack? In the previous section, the bad ideals of the last three rings were non-invertible: $(2, 1 + \sqrt{-3})$, $2\mathbb Z[i]$ and $(x, y)$. In the first two rings an element of $K$ outside the ring but integral over it, $\tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-3}}{2}$ or $i$, was responsible; in $k[x, y]$ the culprit is a chain of primes $0 \subsetneq (x) \subsetneq (x, y)$ of length $2$. The definition rules out exactly these two defects, plus infinite generation. The argument that the three conditions force every ideal to be invertible follows Conrad's handout; the equivalences follow Sutherland (Proposition 2.9, Theorem 3.23), Aitken and the Stacks Project.

blocks.title: Dedekind domain
blocks.body:
A Dedekind domain is an integral domain $A$ that is

1. Noetherian,
2. integrally closed (every $x \in K = \operatorname{Frac} A$ that is a root of a monic polynomial with coefficients in $A$ already lies in $A$), and
3. of Krull dimension at most $1$: every nonzero prime ideal is maximal.

With this definition every field is a Dedekind domain (there are no nonzero primes); some authors exclude fields, see the conventions below. This is the definition taken as primary in Lean's Mathlib, because it is the one usually checked in practice.

blocks.title: Examples and non-examples
blocks.body: Decide which of the following are Dedekind domains: (a) a principal ideal domain, such as $\mathbb Z$, $k[x]$, $\mathbb Z[i]$; (b) a DVR; (c) $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$; (d) $k[x, y]$ and $\mathbb Z[x]$; (e) $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ and $\mathbb Z + 2i\mathbb Z$; (f) the ring $\overline{\mathbb Z}$ of all algebraic integers in $\mathbb C$.
blocks.solution:
(a) Yes. A PID is Noetherian (one generator per ideal). It is a UFD ([[ufds]]), and a UFD is integrally closed: if $p/q$ in lowest terms satisfies a monic equation $x^n + a_1x^{n-1} + \dots + a_n = 0$, then $p^n = -q(a_1p^{n-1} + \dots + a_nq^{n-1})$, so every prime factor of $q$ divides $p$, hence $q$ is a unit. A nonzero prime $(p)$ is maximal: if $(p) \subseteq (q) \ne A$ then $p = qr$ and, $p$ being irreducible and $q$ a non-unit, $r$ is a unit. (Sutherland, Corollary 2.11; Gathmann, Example 13.4.)

(b) Yes: a DVR is a PID.

(c) Yes. $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ is the ring of integers of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5})$ ([[ideals]]), and rings of integers are Dedekind; this is proved in the section on rings of integers below. It is not a UFD, since $2$ is irreducible but not prime (Gathmann, Example 13.6).

(d) No. $k[x, y]$ has the chain $0 \subsetneq (x) \subsetneq (x, y)$, so the nonzero prime $(x)$ is not maximal; likewise $0 \subsetneq (2) \subsetneq (2, x)$ in $\mathbb Z[x]$. Both are Noetherian UFDs (Sutherland, Remark 2.12). Only condition 3 fails.

(e) No. $\theta = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-3}}{2}$ is a root of $x^2 - x + 1$ and lies in $\operatorname{Frac}\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}] = \mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$ but not in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$; and $i$ is a root of $x^2 + 1$, lies in $\operatorname{Frac}(\mathbb Z + 2i\mathbb Z) = \mathbb Q(i)$, but not in $\mathbb Z + 2i\mathbb Z$. Both rings are Noetherian of dimension $1$; only condition 2 fails.

(f) No: $\overline{\mathbb Z}$ is not Noetherian. Taking square roots gives the chain
$$(2) \subsetneq (2^{1/2}) \subsetneq (2^{1/4}) \subsetneq \cdots.$$
Each inclusion holds since $2^{1/2^n} = (2^{1/2^{n+1}})^2$, and it is strict since $2^{1/2^{n+1}}/2^{1/2^n} = 2^{-1/2^{n+1}}$ is not an algebraic integer: its minimal polynomial is $x^{2^{n+1}} - \tfrac12$, which is not in $\mathbb Z[x]$ (and a monic polynomial over $\mathbb Z$ vanishing at an algebraic number is divisible by its minimal polynomial, whose coefficients would then be algebraic integers and rational, hence integers). The ring $\overline{\mathbb Z}$ is integrally closed and every nonzero prime is maximal; only condition 1 fails (Wikipedia).

blocks.caption: Dedekind domains and unique factorisation domains overlap exactly in the principal ideal domains (proved in the section on the class group), and DVRs are the local PIDs that are not fields. $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ and $\mathbb C[E] = \mathbb C[x, y]/(y^2 - x^3 + x)$ are Dedekind but not UFDs (the class group of $\mathbb C[E]$ is the group $E(\mathbb C)$ of the elliptic curve, by Clark); $k[x, y]$ and $\mathbb Z[x]$ are UFDs of dimension $2$; $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ and $\mathbb Z + 2i\mathbb Z$ are not integrally closed and $\overline{\mathbb Z}$ is not Noetherian.

Their overlap is labelled PID and contains Z, k[x], Z[i], and a smaller blue ellipse labelled DVR containing Z_(p). The Dedekind-only part contains Z[sqrt(-5)] and C[E]. The UFD-only part contains k[x,y] and Z[x]. Below both, in red, rings that are neither: Z[sqrt(-3)], Z+2iZ and the ring of all algebraic integers.

blocks.title: Every nonzero ideal contains a product of nonzero primes
blocks.body: Let $A$ be a Noetherian domain that is not a field. Every nonzero ideal $I$ of $A$ contains a product $\mathfrak p_1\cdots\mathfrak p_r$ of nonzero prime ideals ($r \ge 1$).

Idea: a minimal counterexample cannot exist, and Noetherianity provides a maximal one, which is just as good (Conrad, Lemma 6.2, replacing the "smallest index" argument of his Lemma 3.1 by Noetherian induction).

If $I = A$, any nonzero prime will do; one exists because $A$ is not a field, so it has a nonzero maximal ideal. Suppose the set $\Sigma$ of nonzero proper ideals not containing such a product is nonempty. Since $A$ is Noetherian, $\Sigma$ has a maximal element $I$ (see [[noetherian-rings]]). $I$ is not prime (a prime contains itself), and $I \ne A$, so there are $x, y \notin I$ with $xy \in I$. The ideals $I + (x)$ and $I + (y)$ strictly contain $I$ and are nonzero, so they are not in $\Sigma$: each contains a product of nonzero primes (if one of them is $A$, use the remark at the start). Then
$$\begin{aligned}\mathfrak p_1\cdots\mathfrak p_r\,\mathfrak q_1\cdots\mathfrak q_s &\subseteq (I + (x))(I + (y))\\ &\subseteq I + (xy) = I,\end{aligned}$$
contradicting $I \in \Sigma$.

blocks.title: Nonzero primes are invertible
blocks.body: Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain that is not a field and $\mathfrak p$ a nonzero prime ideal. Then $(A : \mathfrak p) \ne A$, and $\mathfrak p\,(A : \mathfrak p) = A$. In particular $\mathfrak p$ is invertible.

Idea: find an element $x \in K \setminus A$ with $x\mathfrak p \subseteq A$; then $\mathfrak p \subseteq \mathfrak p + x\mathfrak p \subseteq A$, and maximality leaves two options. The bad option, $x\mathfrak p \subseteq \mathfrak p$, makes $x$ integral over $A$, which integral closedness forbids. This is Conrad's proof (Theorem 3.2, and Theorem 6.6 for general Dedekind domains); each of the three defining conditions is used once.

Step 1: $(A : \mathfrak p) \ne A$. Pick $0 \ne a \in \mathfrak p$. By the previous theorem $(a)$ contains a product of nonzero primes; choose one, $\mathfrak p_1\cdots\mathfrak p_r \subseteq (a)$, with $r$ minimal. Since $\mathfrak p \supseteq (a) \supseteq \mathfrak p_1\cdots\mathfrak p_r$ and $\mathfrak p$ is prime, $\mathfrak p$ contains some $\mathfrak p_i$ (if $\mathfrak p$ contained none, pick $y_i \in \mathfrak p_i \setminus \mathfrak p$; then $y_1\cdots y_r \in \mathfrak p$, which is impossible). Say $\mathfrak p_1 \subseteq \mathfrak p$; as $\mathfrak p_1$ is a nonzero prime it is maximal (condition 3), so $\mathfrak p_1 = \mathfrak p$.

If $r = 1$, then $\mathfrak p \subseteq (a) \subseteq \mathfrak p$, so $\mathfrak p = (a)$ and $a^{-1} \in (A : \mathfrak p) \setminus A$ ($a$ is not a unit). If $r \ge 2$, by minimality $(a) \not\supseteq \mathfrak p_2\cdots\mathfrak p_r$; pick $b \in \mathfrak p_2\cdots\mathfrak p_r$ with $b \notin (a)$. Then
$$b\,\mathfrak p \subseteq \mathfrak p_1\mathfrak p_2\cdots\mathfrak p_r \subseteq (a),$$
so $x = b/a$ satisfies $x\mathfrak p \subseteq A$, i.e. $x \in (A : \mathfrak p)$, while $x \notin A$ because $b \notin (a)$.

Step 2: $\mathfrak p(A : \mathfrak p) = A$. Take $x \in (A : \mathfrak p) \setminus A$. Then $\mathfrak p \subseteq \mathfrak p + x\mathfrak p \subseteq A$, and $\mathfrak p + x\mathfrak p$ is an ideal of $A$; since $\mathfrak p$ is maximal it is $\mathfrak p$ or $A$.

Suppose it were $\mathfrak p$, i.e. $x\mathfrak p \subseteq \mathfrak p$. Let $g_1, \dots, g_n$ generate $\mathfrak p$ (condition 1). Then $xg_i = \sum_j a_{ij}g_j$ with $a_{ij} \in A$, so the matrix $M = xI_n - (a_{ij})$ over the field $K$ kills the nonzero vector $(g_1, \dots, g_n)^T$. Hence $\det M = 0$, and expanding the determinant gives a monic polynomial of degree $n$ with coefficients in $A$ that vanishes at $x$. So $x$ is integral over $A$, and $x \in A$ by condition 2, a contradiction.

Hence $\mathfrak p + x\mathfrak p = A$, so $\mathfrak p\cdot(A + xA) = A$: the fractional ideal $A + xA$ is an inverse of $\mathfrak p$, and by part 3 of the basic properties it equals $(A : \mathfrak p)$.

blocks.title: Integrally closed local domains of dimension one are DVRs
blocks.body: Let $(R, \mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local domain of dimension $1$ that is integrally closed. Then $\mathfrak m$ is principal, so $R$ is a DVR. This is the remaining implication (3) implies (2) of the theorem on local rings.

$R$ is a Dedekind domain (Noetherian, integrally closed, its only nonzero prime $\mathfrak m$ is maximal) and not a field. By the previous theorem $\mathfrak m$ is invertible, and in a local domain invertible fractional ideals are principal (part 5 of the basic properties). Now apply the implication (2) implies (1). Aitken proves the same statement this way, without using unique factorisation (his Theorem 45); Sutherland quotes it from his first lecture.

blocks.title: Equivalent definitions of a Dedekind domain

blocks.body:
If $A$ is a field all three conditions hold (there are no nonzero primes and the only fractional ideal is $K = A$), so assume $A$ is not a field. Then every maximal ideal is nonzero.

(1) implies (2). (Sutherland, Proposition 2.9.) Let $\mathfrak p \ne 0$ be prime. By the theorem on what localisation preserves ([[localization]]), $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a Noetherian integrally closed local domain. Its primes correspond to the primes of $A$ inside $\mathfrak p$, which are $0$ and $\mathfrak p$ (a nonzero prime inside $\mathfrak p$ is maximal, so equals $\mathfrak p$); so $\dim A_{\mathfrak p} = 1$. By the previous theorem $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a DVR.

(2) implies (1). A DVR is integrally closed. If $x \in K$ is integral over $A$, it is integral over each $A_{\mathfrak p}$, so $x \in A_{\mathfrak p}$ for every nonzero prime $\mathfrak p$, and $x \in A$ because a domain is the intersection of its localisations at maximal ideals ([[localization]]). For the dimension: a chain $0 \ne \mathfrak q \subsetneq \mathfrak p$ of primes would give a chain $0 \subsetneq \mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p} \subsetneq \mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ in $A_{\mathfrak p}$, but a DVR has only two primes.

(2) implies (3). (Sutherland, Corollary 3.3.) Let $I$ be a nonzero fractional ideal. For each maximal $\mathfrak m$, $I_{\mathfrak m}$ is a nonzero fractional ideal of the DVR $A_{\mathfrak m}$, hence of the form $\pi^kA_{\mathfrak m}$ with $k \in \mathbb Z$ (multiply by a common denominator and use the structure theorem), hence principal. By part 6 of the basic properties, $I$ is invertible.

(3) implies (2). (Aitken, Theorem 69.) Every nonzero ideal is invertible, hence finitely generated (part 4), so $A$ is Noetherian. Let $\mathfrak p \ne 0$ be prime. Every nonzero ideal $J$ of $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is extended from the ideal $J \cap A$ of $A$ ([[localization]]): $J = (J \cap A)A_{\mathfrak p}$. If $L$ is an inverse of $J \cap A$, then $J \cdot LA_{\mathfrak p} = A_{\mathfrak p}$. So every nonzero ideal of the local domain $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is invertible, hence principal (part 5); in particular its maximal ideal $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p} \ne 0$ is principal, and $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a DVR by the theorem on local rings.

items.label: Three conditions
items.body: Noetherian, integrally closed, every nonzero prime maximal. Baanen and coauthors made this the primary definition of Mathlib because it is the one checked in practice, for instance for rings of integers (Wikipedia calls it DD4). It explains which defect each non-example has.

items.label: Locally a DVR
items.body: A Noetherian domain all of whose localisations at nonzero primes are DVRs: Sutherland's Definition 2.10. Gathmann asks for one-dimensional Noetherian domains whose localisations at maximal ideals are regular local rings (Definition 13.1), and shows this is the same as being normal (Lemma 13.3). Locally the ring is as simple as possible; everything interesting is global.

items.label: Ideals form a group
items.body: Every nonzero fractional ideal is invertible (Wikipedia's DD3, Aitken's Theorem 69, Mathlib's second definition). This is the definition that makes the class group a group and that the factorisation proofs actually use.

items.label: Ideals factor uniquely
items.body: The Stacks Project defines a Dedekind domain as a domain in which every nonzero ideal is a product of nonzero primes, uniquely up to order, with no Noetherian hypothesis (Definition 10.120.14), and proves that this forces the other conditions (Lemma 10.120.17). Historically this is the property Dedekind proved for rings of integers, and the axioms are Noether's characterisation of it.

items.label: Krull of dimension one
items.body: Chang and Geroldinger, working in factorisation theory, define Dedekind domains as Krull domains of dimension at most one, equivalently Noetherian domains all of whose localisations at maximal ideals are DVRs; Wikipedia attributes the Krull-domain definition to Bourbaki. This places Dedekind domains among Krull monoids, where the class group governs factorisation of elements.

rows.text: Fields are Dedekind domains (the conditions on nonzero primes are vacuous). Wikipedia notes that many theorems then need only trivial changes for fields.
Gathmann requires dimension exactly $1$, which excludes fields. Sutherland's setting for extensions of Dedekind domains ('AKLB') assumes $A$ is not a field.
Discusses both conventions (Remark 6.4): excluding fields is preferable for geometric reasons, but statements such as 'a Dedekind UFD is a PID' are cleaner if fields are included.

Unique factorisation of ideals (Stacks); Noetherian, integrally closed, dimension at most $1$ (Mathlib, Conrad, Wikipedia DD4); DVR localisations (Sutherland); regular localisations (Gathmann); Krull of dimension at most $1$ (Chang-Geroldinger). All are equivalent by the theorems on this page.
Allows fields, and says 'not a field' wherever it matters.

blocks.title: Where exactly does Z[√−3] fail?
blocks.body: Let $A = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ and $P = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-3})$, the set of $a + b\sqrt{-3}$ with $a \equiv b \pmod 2$. Show that $A_P$ is not a DVR, but that $A_{\mathfrak q}$ is a DVR for every other nonzero prime $\mathfrak q$. (You may use that $\mathbb Z[\theta]$, $\theta = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-3}}{2}$, is a principal ideal domain: these are the Eisenstein integers, see [[eisenstein-integers]].)
blocks.solution:
$A_P$ is not a DVR. In the exercise of the previous section we found $P^2 = 2P$. If $PA_P = \pi A_P$, this gives $\pi^2A_P = 2\pi A_P$, and cancelling $\pi$ (a domain), $PA_P = \pi A_P = 2A_P$. Then $1 + \sqrt{-3} = 2\cdot c/s$ with $c \in A$ and $s \in A \setminus P$, i.e. $s(1 + \sqrt{-3}) \in 2A$. Write $s = c_1 + c_2\sqrt{-3}$; then
$$s(1 + \sqrt{-3}) = (c_1 - 3c_2) + (c_1 + c_2)\sqrt{-3},$$
and both coordinates are even iff $c_1 \equiv c_2 \pmod 2$, i.e. iff $s \in P$. Contradiction. So the maximal ideal of $A_P$ is not principal, and $A_P$ is not a DVR.

The only prime containing $2$ is $P$. Indeed $A/2A \cong \mathbb F_2[x]/(x^2 + 3) = \mathbb F_2[x]/((x + 1)^2)$ has a single prime ideal, the image of $(x + 1)$, which corresponds to $P$.

Every other nonzero prime $\mathfrak q$ is a DVR point. Such $\mathfrak q$ does not contain $2$, so $2$ is a unit in $A_{\mathfrak q}$ and $A_{\mathfrak q}$ is a localisation of $A[1/2]$. But $A[1/2] = \mathbb Z[\theta][1/2]$: one inclusion because $A \subseteq \mathbb Z[\theta]$, the other because $\theta = (1 + \sqrt{-3})/2 \in A[1/2]$. A localisation of the PID $\mathbb Z[\theta]$ is a PID, hence a Dedekind domain, and so is its localisation at the nonzero prime $\mathfrak q A[1/2]$. Therefore $A_{\mathfrak q} = (A[1/2])_{\mathfrak qA[1/2]}$ is a DVR by the equivalence theorem. So $A$ fails to be Dedekind at exactly one point, the prime containing the conductor $2\mathbb Z[\theta]$ of the order (compare Conrad §8, where all but finitely many primes of an order are shown to be invertible).

blocks.body:
- Integrally closed means integrally closed in the ring's own fraction field. $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ is integrally closed in nothing larger than itself, but it misses $\tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-3}}{2}$, which lies in its fraction field.
- A Dedekind domain is generally not a UFD ($\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$), and a UFD is generally not Dedekind ($k[x, y]$). Being both forces being a PID.
- "Dimension at most $1$" is about chains of prime ideals, not about the ring being "one-dimensional" over some field: $\mathbb Z$ and $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ have dimension $1$.
- Local conditions need the Noetherian hypothesis: there are non-Noetherian domains all of whose localisations at maximal ideals are DVRs ("almost Dedekind domains"); they are not Dedekind (Wikipedia; Chang-Geroldinger §2.2).

items.q: Is $\mathbb Z[1/6]$ a Dedekind domain?
items.a: Yes: it is a localisation of $\mathbb Z$, hence a PID. Its maximal ideals are $p\mathbb Z[1/6]$ for primes $p \ne 2, 3$.

items.q: Is $\mathbb Q[x]/(x^2)$ a Dedekind domain?
items.a: No: it is not a domain ($x \cdot x = 0$).

items.q: Which of the three conditions does $\mathbb Z[2i] = \mathbb Z + 2i\mathbb Z$ violate?
items.a: Only integral closedness: $i$ is integral but not in the ring.

items.q: Why does the invertibility proof need $\mathfrak p$ to be finitely generated?
items.a: To turn $x\mathfrak p \subseteq \mathfrak p$ into a monic equation for $x$ by the determinant trick; this needs finitely many generators.

items.q: Which of these rings are Dedekind domains: $\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z$; $\mathbb Z[x]/(x^2 + 1)$; $\mathbb Z_{(7)}$; $\mathbb Q[x, y]/(y)$; $\mathbb Z[\sqrt 5]$?
items.hint: Check the domain condition first, then each of the three conditions.
items.solution: $\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z$: no, not a domain ($(1,0)(0,1) = 0$). $\mathbb Z[x]/(x^2 + 1) \cong \mathbb Z[i]$: yes, a PID. $\mathbb Z_{(7)}$: yes, a DVR. $\mathbb Q[x, y]/(y) \cong \mathbb Q[x]$: yes, a PID. $\mathbb Z[\sqrt 5]$: no, because $\tfrac{1 + \sqrt 5}{2}$ is a root of $x^2 - x - 1$, lies in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt 5)$ and is not in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt 5]$.

items.q: Show that a Dedekind domain with exactly one nonzero prime ideal is a DVR.
items.hint: Such a ring is local.
items.solution: Its maximal ideals are nonzero primes (it is not a field, since it has a nonzero prime), so there is exactly one: the ring is a Noetherian local integrally closed domain of dimension $1$, hence a DVR by the theorem on integrally closed local domains.

items.q: Let $A$ be a Noetherian integrally closed domain and $\mathfrak p$ a prime with $\mathfrak p A_{\mathfrak p}$ the only nonzero prime of $A_{\mathfrak p}$. Show that $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a DVR. Apply this to $A = k[x, y]$ and $\mathfrak p = (x)$.
items.hint: Localisation preserves Noetherian and integrally closed.
items.solution: $A_{\mathfrak p}$ is a Noetherian integrally closed local domain, and its primes are $0$ and $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$, so it has dimension $1$; it is a DVR by the theorem on integrally closed local domains. For $k[x, y]$ (a UFD, hence integrally closed) and $\mathfrak p = (x)$: the primes inside $(x)$ are $0$ and $(x)$ (if $\mathfrak q \subseteq (x)$ is a nonzero prime, some irreducible factor $g$ of a nonzero element of $\mathfrak q$ lies in $\mathfrak q \subseteq (x)$; then $x \mid g$, so $g$ is an associate of $x$, and $(x) \subseteq \mathfrak q$). So $k[x,y]_{(x)}$ is a DVR, with valuation the exponent of $x$ in a fraction; this is the order of vanishing along the line $x = 0$. Being Dedekind fails for $k[x, y]$ only at the maximal ideals.

items.q: Show that $\theta = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt 5}{2}$ is integral over $\mathbb Z$ and deduce that $\mathbb Z[\sqrt 5]$ is not integrally closed. Then show that the prime $P = (2, 1 + \sqrt 5)$ of $\mathbb Z[\sqrt 5]$ is not invertible.
items.hint: Imitate the $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ computation: compute $P^2$.
items.solution: $\theta^2 = \tfrac{6 + 2\sqrt 5}{4} = \theta + 1$, so $\theta^2 - \theta - 1 = 0$, and $\theta \notin \mathbb Z[\sqrt 5]$. As before $P = \{a + b\sqrt 5 : a \equiv b \pmod 2\}$, the kernel of $a + b\sqrt5 \mapsto a - b \bmod 2$ (a ring map since $1^2 \equiv 5 \pmod 2$). Now $(1 + \sqrt 5)^2 = 6 + 2\sqrt 5 = 2(3 + \sqrt 5)$ with $3 + \sqrt 5 \in P$, and $$\begin{aligned}P^2 &= (4,\ 2 + 2\sqrt 5,\ 6 + 2\sqrt 5)\\ &= 2(2,\ 1 + \sqrt 5,\ 3 + \sqrt 5) = 2P.\end{aligned}$$ If $P$ were invertible, cancelling $P$ would give $P = (2)$, but $(2)$ has index $4$ and $P$ index $2$. So $P$ is not invertible.

items.q: Show that the ring $\overline{\mathbb Z}$ of all algebraic integers is integrally closed in its fraction field $\overline{\mathbb Q}$, and that it is not a Dedekind domain.
items.hint: Use transitivity of integrality: an element integral over a ring that is integral over $\mathbb Z$ is integral over $\mathbb Z$.
items.solution: $\operatorname{Frac}\overline{\mathbb Z} = \overline{\mathbb Q}$, since every algebraic number $\alpha$ has a nonzero integer multiple $d\alpha$ that is an algebraic integer (clear the leading coefficient of its minimal polynomial as in the section on rings of integers). If $x \in \overline{\mathbb Q}$ is integral over $\overline{\mathbb Z}$, it satisfies a monic equation with coefficients $c_1, \dots, c_n \in \overline{\mathbb Z}$; then $\mathbb Z[c_1, \dots, c_n, x]$ is a finitely generated $\mathbb Z$-module (each generator is integral over the previous ring), so $x$ is integral over $\mathbb Z$ by the determinant trick, i.e. $x \in \overline{\mathbb Z}$. It is not Dedekind because it is not Noetherian: the chain $(2) \subsetneq (2^{1/2}) \subsetneq (2^{1/4}) \subsetneq \cdots$ of the example above never stabilises.

blocks.body:
- Dedekind domain: Noetherian, integrally closed, every nonzero prime maximal.
- Key steps: every nonzero ideal contains a product of nonzero primes; every nonzero prime is invertible (integral closedness kills the bad case $x\mathfrak p \subseteq \mathfrak p$).
- Equivalent: Noetherian with DVR localisations; every nonzero fractional ideal invertible.
- Examples: PIDs, DVRs, rings of integers, localisations of these. Non-examples: $k[x, y]$, $\mathbb Z[x]$ (dimension), $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$, $\mathbb Z[\sqrt 5]$, $\mathbb Z + 2i\mathbb Z$ (integral closure), $\overline{\mathbb Z}$ (Noetherian).
- An order like $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ fails only at the primes containing its conductor.

blocks.title: Unique factorisation of ideals and valuations
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to factor ideals in a Dedekind domain, compute with the exponents $v_{\mathfrak p}$, and translate freely between containment and divisibility of ideals.

The question: on [[ideals]] we found $(6) = P_2^2P_3P_3'$ in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$. Why is there no other factorisation of $(6)$ into prime ideals, and why does every ideal factor at all? With invertible primes, the proofs are those for integers: existence by peeling off one prime at a time, uniqueness by cancelling. We follow Conrad (Theorems 3.6, 4.3, Corollary 4.5), and compare with Sutherland's local proof and Gathmann's proof by primary decomposition.

blocks.title: Unique factorisation of ideals
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain. Every nonzero proper ideal $I$ of $A$ is a product of nonzero prime ideals,
$$I = \mathfrak p_1\mathfrak p_2\cdots\mathfrak p_r,$$
and this factorisation is unique up to the order of the factors.

Idea: existence by induction on the length of a product of primes contained in $I$, dividing out one prime at a time; uniqueness by cancelling primes, which are invertible. This is Conrad's Theorem 3.6 (Theorem 6.7 for general Dedekind domains). We may assume $A$ is not a field (otherwise there are no nonzero proper ideals). Two facts are used: a prime containing a product of ideals contains one of the factors (shown in the proof of invertibility of primes), and nonzero primes are maximal.

Existence. By the theorem on products of primes, $I$ contains some product $\mathfrak p_1\cdots\mathfrak p_r$ of nonzero primes; we induct on $r$. If $r = 1$, $\mathfrak p_1 \subseteq I \ne A$ and $\mathfrak p_1$ is maximal, so $I = \mathfrak p_1$. If $r > 1$, choose a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m \supseteq I$. Then $\mathfrak m \supseteq \mathfrak p_1\cdots\mathfrak p_r$, so $\mathfrak m \supseteq \mathfrak p_i$ for some $i$, and $\mathfrak m = \mathfrak p_i$ by maximality; say $i = 1$. Multiply $\mathfrak p_1 \supseteq I \supseteq \mathfrak p_1\mathfrak p_2\cdots\mathfrak p_r$ by $\mathfrak p_1^{-1}$:
$$A \supseteq \mathfrak p_1^{-1}I \supseteq \mathfrak p_2\cdots\mathfrak p_r.$$
So $J = \mathfrak p_1^{-1}I$ is an ideal of $A$ containing a product of $r - 1$ primes. If $J = A$ then $I = \mathfrak p_1$; otherwise $J$ is a product of primes by induction, and so is $I = \mathfrak p_1J$.

Uniqueness. Suppose $\mathfrak p_1\cdots\mathfrak p_r = \mathfrak q_1\cdots\mathfrak q_s$ with all factors nonzero primes; induct on $r$. If $r = 0$ the left side is $A$, which forces $s = 0$ (a product of proper ideals is proper). If $r \ge 1$, $\mathfrak p_1 \supseteq \mathfrak q_1\cdots\mathfrak q_s$, so $s \ge 1$ and $\mathfrak p_1 \supseteq \mathfrak q_j$ for some $j$; since $\mathfrak q_j$ is maximal, $\mathfrak p_1 = \mathfrak q_j$. Multiplying by $\mathfrak p_1^{-1}$ cancels it from both sides, and the induction hypothesis applies.

blocks.title: The group of fractional ideals and the valuations
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$.

1. The nonzero fractional ideals form an abelian group $\mathcal I_A$ under multiplication, with identity $A$. Every $I \in \mathcal I_A$ can be written uniquely as
$$I = \prod_{\mathfrak p} \mathfrak p^{v_{\mathfrak p}(I)},$$
over the nonzero primes, with integers $v_{\mathfrak p}(I)$, almost all $0$. So $\mathcal I_A$ is the free abelian group on the nonzero primes.
2. $v_{\mathfrak p}(IJ) = v_{\mathfrak p}(I) + v_{\mathfrak p}(J)$, and $v_{\mathfrak p}(I)$ equals the exponent $k$ with $IA_{\mathfrak p} = (\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p})^k$ in the DVR $A_{\mathfrak p}$.
3. For $x \in K^\times$ put $v_{\mathfrak p}(x) = v_{\mathfrak p}(xA)$. This is the discrete valuation of the DVR $A_{\mathfrak p}$, and $A = \{x \in K : v_{\mathfrak p}(x) \ge 0 \text{ for all } \mathfrak p\}$.

1. Every nonzero fractional ideal is invertible (equivalence theorem), and products of fractional ideals are fractional ideals, so $\mathcal I_A$ is a group. Write $I = d^{-1}J$ with $0 \ne d \in A$ and $J = dI$ an ideal of $A$. Factor $J$ and $(d)$ into primes; then $I = J\,(d)^{-1}$ is a product of primes with integer exponents. If two such products agree, move the negative exponents to the other side: we get an equality of two products of primes with nonnegative exponents, which by the previous theorem have the same exponents. (Conrad, Corollary 4.2; Sutherland, Theorem 3.11.)

2. Additivity is clear from uniqueness. For the local statement: localisation is multiplicative, $(IJ)A_{\mathfrak p} = (IA_{\mathfrak p})(JA_{\mathfrak p})$ (also for inverses, since $I I^{-1} = A$ localises to $A_{\mathfrak p}$). For a nonzero prime $\mathfrak q \ne \mathfrak p$, $\mathfrak q \not\subseteq \mathfrak p$ (both are maximal), so $\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p} = A_{\mathfrak p}$. Hence
$$IA_{\mathfrak p} = \prod_{\mathfrak q} (\mathfrak qA_{\mathfrak p})^{v_{\mathfrak q}(I)} = (\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p})^{v_{\mathfrak p}(I)}.$$
The powers of $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p} = \pi A_{\mathfrak p}$ with integer exponents are distinct (structure of DVRs), so the exponent is determined.

3. By part 2, $xA_{\mathfrak p} = \pi^{v_{\mathfrak p}(x)}A_{\mathfrak p}$, i.e. $v_{\mathfrak p}(x)$ is the DVR valuation of $x$ (write $x = u\pi^k$). Finally $x \in A$ iff $x \in A_{\mathfrak p}$ for every nonzero $\mathfrak p$ (a domain is the intersection of its localisations at maximal ideals, [[localization]]) iff all $v_{\mathfrak p}(x) \ge 0$.

blocks.title: To contain is to divide
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain and $I, J$ nonzero fractional ideals.

1. $I \subseteq J$ iff $v_{\mathfrak p}(I) \ge v_{\mathfrak p}(J)$ for all $\mathfrak p$ iff $I = JL$ for an integral ideal $L$ (i.e. $J$ divides $I$).
2. $v_{\mathfrak p}(I + J) = \min(v_{\mathfrak p}(I), v_{\mathfrak p}(J))$ and $v_{\mathfrak p}(I \cap J) = \max(v_{\mathfrak p}(I), v_{\mathfrak p}(J))$. So $I + J$ is the greatest common divisor and $I \cap J$ the least common multiple, and
$$(I + J)(I \cap J) = IJ.$$

1. If $I \subseteq J$, put $L = J^{-1}I$; then $L \subseteq J^{-1}J = A$ is an integral ideal and $JL = I$, so $v_{\mathfrak p}(I) = v_{\mathfrak p}(J) + v_{\mathfrak p}(L) \ge v_{\mathfrak p}(J)$ (an integral ideal has nonnegative exponents). If all $v_{\mathfrak p}(I) \ge v_{\mathfrak p}(J)$, then $L = \prod\mathfrak p^{v_{\mathfrak p}(I) - v_{\mathfrak p}(J)}$ is a product of integral ideals, so $L \subseteq A$ and $I = JL \subseteq JA = J$. (Conrad, Theorem 4.3.)

2. Let $M = \prod\mathfrak p^{\min(v_{\mathfrak p}(I), v_{\mathfrak p}(J))}$. By part 1, $M \supseteq I$ and $M \supseteq J$, so $M \supseteq I + J$, giving $v_{\mathfrak p}(I + J) \ge \min$. And $I + J \supseteq I$, $I + J \supseteq J$ give $v_{\mathfrak p}(I + J) \le v_{\mathfrak p}(I)$ and $\le v_{\mathfrak p}(J)$. The intersection is analogous with $\max$: by part 1 a fractional ideal is contained in both $I$ and $J$ iff its exponents are at least the maximum, and $I \cap J$ is the largest such. The last identity is $\min + \max = $ sum. (Conrad, Corollary 4.5; Gathmann, Proposition 13.13.)

items.label: Invert primes, cancel
items.body: Show that every nonzero ideal contains a product of primes and that every nonzero prime is invertible, then argue as for integers: peel off primes for existence, cancel for uniqueness. This is Conrad's route, followed above; Mathlib's formalisation proves invertibility of all nonzero ideals at once by the same integrality argument.

items.label: Local exponents
items.body: Sutherland (Theorem 3.11) works locally: for each nonzero prime the DVR $A_{\mathfrak p}$ gives an exponent $v_{\mathfrak p}(I)$; only finitely many are nonzero, and $I \mapsto (v_{\mathfrak p}(I))_{\mathfrak p}$ is injective because $I = \bigcap_{\mathfrak p} IA_{\mathfrak p}$ and $IA_{\mathfrak p}$ is determined by the exponent. Surjectivity onto finitely supported vectors is checked on products of primes. Factorisation becomes 'an ideal is its vector of local exponents'.

items.label: Primary decomposition
items.body: Gathmann (Proposition 13.7) uses the primary decomposition of $I$ from general commutative algebra: in a Dedekind domain the associated primes of $I$ are maximal, the $\mathfrak p$-primary ideals are exactly the powers $\mathfrak p^k$ (localise at $\mathfrak p$, where ideals are powers of the maximal ideal), and pairwise coprime ideals have intersection equal to their product.

blocks.title: Gcd and lcm in Z[√−5]
blocks.body: In $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ compute $(2) + (1 + \sqrt{-5})$ and $(2) \cap (1 + \sqrt{-5})$ as products of primes, find generators, and check $(I + J)(I \cap J) = IJ$.
blocks.solution:
From [[ideals]]: $(2) = P_2^2$ and $(1 + \sqrt{-5}) = P_2P_3$. Exponents at $(P_2, P_3)$: $(2, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$. So
$$(2) + (1 + \sqrt{-5}) = P_2^{\min(2,1)}P_3^{\min(0,1)} = P_2,$$
which is visibly right: the sum is $(2, 1 + \sqrt{-5}) = P_2$ by definition. And
$$(2) \cap (1 + \sqrt{-5}) = P_2^2P_3 = (2)P_3 = (6, 2 + 2\sqrt{-5}).$$
Check of the identity: $(I + J)(I \cap J) = P_2 \cdot P_2^2P_3 = P_2^3P_3$ and $IJ = P_2^2 \cdot P_2P_3 = P_2^3P_3$. One can also verify $(2) \cap (1 + \sqrt{-5}) = (6, 2 + 2\sqrt{-5})$ directly as lattices: both have index $12$ in $D$ (norm $4 \cdot 3$), and $6 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5})$ and $2 + 2\sqrt{-5}$ lie in both ideals.

blocks.title: Orders of vanishing on a cubic curve
blocks.body:
Let $R = \mathbb C[x, y]/(y^2 - x^3 + x)$, the coordinate ring of the smooth curve $X: y^2 = x(x - 1)(x + 1)$; it is a Dedekind domain (Gathmann, Example 13.4(b) and Example 13.12). Write $\mathfrak m_{(a,b)} = (x - a, y - b)$ for the maximal ideal of the point $(a, b) \in X$. Show that
$$(x) = \mathfrak m_{(0,0)}^2, \qquad (y) = \mathfrak m_{(0,0)}\,\mathfrak m_{(1,0)}\,\mathfrak m_{(-1,0)},$$
and interpret the exponents.
blocks.solution:
Write $\mathfrak m = \mathfrak m_{(0,0)} = (x, y)$ and use $y^2 = x(x^2 - 1)$ in $R$.

$(x) = \mathfrak m^2$: $\mathfrak m^2 = (x^2, xy, y^2) = (x^2, xy, x(x^2 - 1)) \subseteq (x)$. Conversely
$$x = x\cdot x^2 - x(x^2 - 1) = x^2\cdot x - y^2 \in \mathfrak m^2.$$
So $(x) = \mathfrak m^2$.

$(y)$: the zeros of $y$ on $X$ are the points with $y = 0$, so $x(x - 1)(x + 1) = 0$: the three points $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, $(-1,0)$. Let $M = \mathfrak m_{(0,0)}\mathfrak m_{(1,0)}\mathfrak m_{(-1,0)}$. Distinct maximal ideals are pairwise coprime, so $M$ is also their intersection, and $y \in M$ because $y$ lies in all three; so $(y) \subseteq M$. Now compare quotients. $R/(y) \cong \mathbb C[x, y]/(y, x^3 - x) \cong \mathbb C[x]/(x^3 - x)$ has dimension $3$ over $\mathbb C$, and $R/M \cong \mathbb C^3$ by the Chinese remainder theorem (next sections), also of dimension $3$. The surjection $R/(y) \to R/M$ is a linear map between spaces of the same finite dimension, hence injective, so $(y) = M$. (The computer check below confirms both identities with Gr\"obner bases.)

Interpretation (Gathmann, Remark 13.11): the exponent of $\mathfrak m_P$ in $(f)$ is the order of vanishing of $f$ at $P$. The function $x$ vanishes at $(0,0)$ only, to order $2$, because the line $x = 0$ is tangent to $X$ there; the function $y$ vanishes simply at the three points where the line $y = 0$ crosses $X$. The ideal factorisation of $(f)$ is the divisor of zeros of $f$.
