blocks.title: What is and is not special about rings of integers
blocks.body:
1. (Finiteness.) If $K$ is a number field, $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathcal O_K)$ is finite. The classical proof uses Minkowski's bound (see [[class-group]]); Mathlib's proof, which also covers function fields, replaces it by a pigeonhole argument with "admissible absolute values".
2. (Primes in every class.) If $K$ is a number field, every ideal class of $\mathcal O_K$ contains infinitely many prime ideals; in fact the classes of primes become equidistributed in $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathcal O_K)$ as the norm grows. The proof uses $L$-functions of class group characters (see [[hecke-l]] and [[class-field-theory]]).
3. (Claborn.) For every abelian group $G$ there is a Dedekind domain $A$ with $\operatorname{Cl}(A) \cong G$. Leedham-Green showed $A$ can be taken to be the integral closure of a PID in a quadratic extension, and Clark that it can be taken to be an "elliptic" Dedekind domain.
4. (Failure of 2 in general.) Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over a field $k$ with origin $O$, and $k[E]$ the ring of functions on $E$ regular away from $O$. Then $k[E]$ is a Dedekind domain with $\operatorname{Pic}(k[E]) \cong E(k)$. If $k$ is algebraically closed, the maximal ideals correspond to the points $P \ne O$, the class of the maximal ideal of $P$ corresponds to $P \in E(k)$, and so the trivial class contains no prime at all.

Proofs are not given here. 1: see [[class-group]] and Baanen et al. §8.2. 2: Gargava et al. use the equidistribution in their §2.2; Clark (§2.3) calls the existence of primes in every class a weak form of the Chebotarev density theorem. 3 and 4: Claborn (1966) and Clark (§1, §2.4, Theorem 12); Gathmann's Example 13.29 shows for the plane cubic $y^2 = x(x-1)(x-\lambda)$ how the group law on the curve arises from the Picard group of its coordinate ring.

blocks.title: What does the class group measure?

items.label: Distance from a PID
items.body: $\operatorname{Cl}(A)$ is trivial iff $A$ is a PID iff $A$ is a UFD, so it measures how far ideal factorisation is from element factorisation (Sutherland, Remark 2.25; Gathmann, Remark 13.26).

items.label: Divisors modulo principal divisors
items.body: For the coordinate ring of a smooth curve, a nonzero fractional ideal is a divisor (a formal combination of points, by the factorisation into maximal ideals) and a principal ideal is the divisor of a function. $\operatorname{Pic}$ is divisors modulo divisors of functions; for an elliptic curve minus its origin it is the group of points (Gathmann, Example 13.29; Clark §2.4).

items.label: Rank one projective modules
items.body: An invertible ideal is the same as a finitely generated module that is locally free of rank $1$ (Stacks Lemma 10.120.16 for ideals with $IJ$ principal; the module section below). So $\operatorname{Cl}(A)$ classifies rank one projective $A$-modules up to isomorphism, which is why it is also called the Picard group.

items.label: Factorisation of elements
items.body: In factorisation theory the multiplicative monoid of a Dedekind domain transfers to the monoid of zero-sum sequences over the class group, so arithmetic invariants such as sets of lengths depend only on $\operatorname{Cl}(A)$ and on which classes contain primes (Chang-Geroldinger §4). For example $\mathcal O_K$ is half-factorial (all factorisations of an element into irreducibles have the same length) iff $h_K \le 2$, a theorem of Carlitz quoted by Coykendall-Kettinger.

items.label: Shapes of lattices
items.body: For module lattices over $\mathcal O_K$, the class of the Steinitz ideal is an invariant, and Gargava et al. show that the space of module lattices of rank $t$ has one component for each element of $\operatorname{cl}(K)$.

rows.text: $\operatorname{cl}(A)$ or $\operatorname{Pic}(A)$, ideal group $\mathcal I_A$, principal ideals $\mathcal P_A$.
$\operatorname{Div} R$ (invertible ideals), $\operatorname{Prin} R$, $\operatorname{Pic} R = \operatorname{Div} R/\operatorname{Prin} R$.
$\operatorname{Cl}_K$ or $\operatorname{Cl}(D)$, $h_K$; $\operatorname{cl}(K)$ for the class group of $\mathcal O_K$.

$\operatorname{Pic}(D) = \operatorname{Cl}_d(D)$, with $t$- and $v$-class groups $\operatorname{Cl}_t$, $\operatorname{Cl}_v$ that agree with $\operatorname{Pic}$ for Dedekind domains; the group law is written additively, as usual in factorisation theory.

Also use the narrow class group of a real quadratic field, where only principal ideals with a totally positive generator count as trivial; it can be twice as large as $\operatorname{Cl}$. See [[class-field-theory]].

blocks.body:
- "Every class contains a prime" is a theorem about rings of integers (and more generally global fields), not about Dedekind domains: it fails for $k[E]$ with $k$ algebraically closed. Papers on general Dedekind domains state it as a hypothesis (Chang-Geroldinger construct domains where it holds).
- For a domain that is not Dedekind, the class group is built from invertible ideals only; non-invertible ideals such as $2\mathbb Z[i] \subseteq \mathbb Z + 2i\mathbb Z$ have no class.
- $[I] = [J]$ means $I = xJ$ with $x$ in the fraction field, not in $A$. For integral ideals this is $(\alpha)I = (\beta)J$ with $\alpha, \beta \in A$.

items.q: In $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, which class does $P_3P_7'$ belong to?
items.a: The trivial class: $[P_3][P_7'] = [P_2]^2 = 1$; indeed it has norm $21$ and all ideals of norm $21$ are principal.

items.q: Is $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[i])$ trivial? And $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z_{(3)} \cap \mathbb Z_{(5)})$?
items.a: Both are trivial: both rings are PIDs.

items.q: If $\operatorname{Cl}(A)$ has order $h$, what can you say about $I^h$?
items.a: It is principal for every nonzero fractional ideal $I$ (Lagrange's theorem in $\operatorname{Cl}(A)$).

items.q: Why is the trivial class of $\mathbb C[E]$ free of primes?
items.a: Primes are maximal ideals of points $P \ne O$, and the class of such a prime corresponds to the point $P \ne O$ of $E(\mathbb C) \cong \operatorname{Pic}$, which is not the identity.

items.q: Show directly that $[P_7] = [P_2]$ in $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}])$ by finding $x \in K^\times$ with $P_7 = xP_2$.
items.solution: From $P_2P_7 = (3 + \sqrt{-5})$ ([[ideals]]), $P_7 = (3 + \sqrt{-5})P_2^{-1} = (3 + \sqrt{-5})\cdot\tfrac12P_2$. So $x = \tfrac{3 + \sqrt{-5}}{2}$ works.

items.q: Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain with class number $h$. Show that for every nonzero ideal $I$ and every integer $m$ prime to $h$, if $I^m$ is principal then $I$ is principal.
items.hint: Write $1 = um + vh$.
items.solution: $[I]^h = 1$ by Lagrange and $[I]^m = 1$ by assumption, so $[I] = [I]^{um + vh} = 1$.

items.q: Use the lattice argument to show that $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-2}]$ is a PID.
items.hint: The fundamental rectangle has sides $1$ and $\sqrt 2$; how far is any point of it from the nearest corner?
items.solution: Normalise as in step 1: $1 \in J$, $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-2}] \subseteq J$, and nonzero elements of $J$ have absolute value $\ge 1$. Every point of the rectangle with corners $0, 1, \sqrt{-2}, 1 + \sqrt{-2}$ is within half the diagonal, $\tfrac12\sqrt{1 + 2} = \tfrac{\sqrt 3}{2} < 1$, of some corner (the nearest corner is at most half the width and half the height away in each coordinate). So by step 2 every $z \in J$ is a lattice point: $J = D$, and every fractional ideal is principal. (For $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ half the diagonal is exactly $1$ and the argument breaks down at the centre $\tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-3}}{2}$, the element by which $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-3}]$ fails to be integrally closed.)

items.q: Show that $6$ has exactly two factorisations into irreducible elements of $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, up to order and signs, and that both have length $2$. Relate this to Carlitz's theorem.
items.hint: An irreducible factor of $6$ has norm dividing $36$ and greater than $1$; list the elements of norm $4, 6, 9$.
items.solution: Norms: $N(6) = 36$, and a proper factorisation $6 = \alpha\beta$ into non-units has $N(\alpha)N(\beta) = 36$ with both norms $> 1$; no element has norm $2$ or $3$, so the pairs of norms are $(4, 9)$, $(6, 6)$, $(9, 4)$. Elements of norm $4$: $\pm 2$; norm $6$: $\pm 1 \pm \sqrt{-5}$; norm $9$: $\pm 3, \pm 2 \pm \sqrt{-5}$. All are irreducible (a factor would have norm $2$ or $3$). Checking which products give $6$: $2 \cdot 3$ and $(1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5})$ up to signs; $2 \pm \sqrt{-5}$ do not divide $6$, since $6/(2 + \sqrt{-5}) = \tfrac{6(2 - \sqrt{-5})}{9} \notin D$, and similarly for $2 - \sqrt{-5}$. Both factorisations have length $2$: $D$ is half-factorial, as Carlitz's theorem predicts for class number $h = 2$ (Coykendall-Kettinger, §2). In ideal terms: an irreducible element generates either a principal prime or a product of two primes from the non-trivial class, which makes lengths well defined when $h = 2$.

items.q: Adapt the lattice argument to show $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-6}]) \cong \mathbb Z/2$, generated by the class of $Q = (2, \sqrt{-6})$.
items.hint: The rectangle now has height $\sqrt 6$. The discs of radius $1$ at the corners and of radius $\tfrac12$ at the midpoints of the vertical sides and at the centre again cover it. Which of these three midpoints can lie in $J$?
items.solution:
Normalise $J$ as before, so $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-6}] \subseteq J$ and nonzero elements have absolute value $\ge 1$. The same reasoning as in steps 2 and 3 shows that every $z \in J$ is congruent modulo $D$ to $0$, to $m_1 = \tfrac12\sqrt{-6}$, or to $m_2 = \tfrac12(1 + \sqrt{-6})$, provided the discs cover the rectangle $[0, 1] \times [0, \sqrt 6]$. Covering (by the symmetries reduce to $0 \le s \le \tfrac12$, $0 \le t \le \tfrac{\sqrt6}{2} \approx 1.225$): for $t \le 0.85$, $s^2 + t^2 \le 0.25 + 0.7225 < 1$; for $0.85 \le t \le 1.225$, the distance to the nearer of $(0, \tfrac{\sqrt6}2)$, $(\tfrac12, \tfrac{\sqrt6}2)$ is at most $\sqrt{0.0625 + 0.375^2} = \sqrt{0.203} < \tfrac12$.

Now $m_2 \notin J$: otherwise $m_2(1 - \sqrt{-6}) = \tfrac72 \in J$ and $\tfrac72 - 3 = \tfrac12 \in J$, too small. But $m_1$ is allowed: $m_1\sqrt{-6} = -3 \in D$ gives no contradiction. So $J = D$ or $J = D + \mathbb Zm_1 = \tfrac12(2\mathbb Z + \mathbb Z\sqrt{-6}) = \tfrac12 Q$ (here $Q = (2, \sqrt{-6}) = \{a + b\sqrt{-6} : a \text{ even}\}$, of index $2$). $Q$ is not principal since $a^2 + 6b^2 = 2$ has no solution, and $Q^2 = (4, 2\sqrt{-6}, -6) = (2)$. So $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-6}]) = \{1, [Q]\} \cong \mathbb Z/2$.

blocks.body:
- $\operatorname{Cl}(A) = \operatorname{Pic}(A)$ = invertible fractional ideals modulo principal ones; exact sequence $1 \to A^\times \to K^\times \to \mathcal I_A \to \operatorname{Cl}(A) \to 1$.
- For a Dedekind domain: PID iff UFD iff $\operatorname{Cl}(A) = 1$.
- $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]) \cong \mathbb Z/2$ by a lattice argument; $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-2}]$ is a PID; $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-6}]) \cong \mathbb Z/2$.
- For rings of integers the class group is finite and every class contains infinitely many primes; neither holds for general Dedekind domains (Claborn, Clark).

blocks.title: Localising a Dedekind domain
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to compute the class group of a localisation such as $D[1/\alpha]$, describe rings between a Dedekind domain and its fraction field as intersections of local rings, and avoid a trap in comparing $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ with $\mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)]$.

Why: inverting an element can only make ideals more principal. In $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, inverting $2$ makes $P_2$ the unit ideal; does it make every ideal principal? Coykendall and Kettinger study exactly such rings $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ and their class groups under Galois action. Recall from [[localization]]: for $0 \notin S$, $S^{-1}D$ is again a Dedekind domain; its primes are the $\mathfrak pS^{-1}D$ with $\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing$; extension of ideals is multiplicative; and every ideal of $S^{-1}D$ is extended from an ideal of $D$. We follow Clark (Theorem 5) for the class group and Coykendall-Kettinger (§4-5) for the applications.

blocks.title: Class group of a localisation (Claborn)
blocks.body:
Let $D$ be a Dedekind domain and $S \subseteq D$ multiplicative with $0 
otin S$. The map $[I] \mapsto [IS^{-1}D]$ is a surjective homomorphism $\operatorname{Cl}(D) 	o \operatorname{Cl}(S^{-1}D)$ whose kernel is the subgroup generated by the classes of the primes $\mathfrak p$ with $\mathfrak p \cap S 
e \varnothing$. In particular, if $0 
e \alpha \in D$ is a non-unit with $(\alpha) = \mathfrak p_1^{n_1}\cdots\mathfrak p_k^{n_k}$, then
$$\operatorname{Cl}(D[1/\alpha]) \cong \operatorname{Cl}(D)/\langle[\mathfrak p_1], \dots, [\mathfrak p_k]angle.$$

Idea: on ideal groups, localisation is the projection of a free abelian group onto the summand spanned by the primes that survive. We follow Clark's proof of his Theorem 5 (stated for all overrings); Coykendall and Kettinger's Theorem 4.1 is the case $S = \{\alpha^n\}$. Write $R = S^{-1}D$.

1. Extension $I \mapsto IR$ is a homomorphism $\mathcal I_D \to \mathcal I_R$: if $I = d^{-1}J$ with $J$ an ideal of $D$, then $IR = d^{-1}(JR)$ is a nonzero fractional ideal, and $(IJ)R = (IR)(JR)$. It maps $xD$ to $xR$, so it induces $\operatorname{Cl}(D) \to \operatorname{Cl}(R)$.
2. Surjective: a fractional ideal of $R$ is $d^{-1}J'$ with $J'$ an ideal of $R$ (take $d \in D$), and $J' = (J' \cap D)R$ is extended.
3. On primes: if $\mathfrak p \cap S \ne \varnothing$ then $\mathfrak pR = R$; if $\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing$ then $\mathfrak pR$ is a nonzero prime of $R$, and distinct such $\mathfrak p$ give distinct primes. So in terms of the free bases, $\mathcal I_D \to \mathcal I_R$ sends $\prod\mathfrak p^{n_{\mathfrak p}}$ to $\prod_{\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing}(\mathfrak pR)^{n_{\mathfrak p}}$, and its kernel is the subgroup $\mathcal H$ generated by the primes meeting $S$.
4. Kernel on class groups: the classes of the primes meeting $S$ map to $[R] = 1$. Conversely, if $IR = xR$ with $x \in K^\times$, then $(x^{-1}I)R = R$, so $x^{-1}I \in \mathcal H$ by step 3, and $[I] = [x^{-1}I]$ lies in the subgroup generated by the classes of primes meeting $S$.

For $S = \{1, \alpha, \alpha^2, \dots\}$: $\mathfrak p$ meets $S$ iff $\alpha^n \in \mathfrak p$ for some $n$ iff $\alpha \in \mathfrak p$ iff $\mathfrak p$ divides $(\alpha)$.

blocks.title: Inverting 2 in Z[√−5]
blocks.body: Compute $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}][1/2])$, and verify by hand that the non-principal prime $P_3' = (3, 1 - \sqrt{-5})$ becomes principal in $D[1/2]$.
blocks.solution:
(This is our application of the theorem; Coykendall and Kettinger's own examples invert other elements.) $\operatorname{Cl}(D) \cong \mathbb Z/2$, generated by $[P_2]$. Since $(2) = P_2^2$, the theorem gives $\operatorname{Cl}(D[1/2]) \cong \operatorname{Cl}(D)/\langle[P_2]\rangle = 1$: the ring $D[1/2]$ is a PID.

By hand: $P_2P_3' = (1 - \sqrt{-5})$ in $D$ ([[ideals]]). Extension is multiplicative, and $P_2D[1/2] = D[1/2]$ because $2 \in P_2$ is a unit of $D[1/2]$. So
$$P_3'D[1/2] = (P_2P_3')D[1/2] = (1 - \sqrt{-5})D[1/2].$$

blocks.title: A localisation is the intersection of its local rings
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a domain with fraction field $K$ and $S$ multiplicative with $0 \notin S$. Inside $K$,
$$S^{-1}A = \bigcap_{\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing} A_{\mathfrak p},$$
the intersection over the primes of $A$ disjoint from $S$. For a Dedekind domain $D$ and $R = S^{-1}D$ this is the formula $R = \bigcap_{\mathfrak pR \ne R} D_{\mathfrak p}$, which Coykendall and Kettinger quote from Gilmer (their Proposition 5.2) for every ring $R$ between $D$ and $K$; the case proved here is the one used in their Theorem 5.5, where $R = D[1/a]$.

Put $B = S^{-1}A \subseteq K$, a domain with fraction field $K$. A domain is the intersection of its localisations at its primes ([[localization]]), so $B =  igcap_Q B_Q$ over the primes $Q$ of $B$, and these are the $Q = S^{-1}\mathfrak p$ with $\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing$. It remains to see $B_Q = A_{\mathfrak p}$ inside $K$. If $t \in A \setminus \mathfrak p$ then $t/1 
otin Q$, so $A_{\mathfrak p} \subseteq B_Q$. Conversely an element of $B_Q$ is $b/c$ with $b = a/s$, $c = a'/s'$, $a, a' \in A$, $s, s' \in S$ and $c 
otin Q$; then $a' 
otin \mathfrak p$, and $b/c = (as')/(sa')$ with $sa' 
otin \mathfrak p$ because $s 
otin \mathfrak p$. So $b/c \in A_{\mathfrak p}$.

blocks.title: Inverting an element versus inverting its norm
blocks.body: Coykendall and Kettinger's Theorem 4.2 states that for a number field $K$ and $0 \ne \alpha \in \mathcal O_K$, the ring $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ is the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/N(\alpha)]$ in $K$. Test this on $K = \mathbb Q(i)$, $\alpha = 2 + i$, $N(\alpha) = 5$, and then compare $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ and $\mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)]$ in general.
blocks.solution:
By the theorem on what localisation preserves ([[localization]], with $A = \mathbb Z$, $B = K$, integral closure $\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[i]$ and $S = \{5^n\}$), the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/5]$ in $K$ is $\mathbb Z[i][1/5]$. It contains $R = \mathbb Z[i][1/(2 + i)]$, since $1/(2 + i) = (2 - i)/5$. But it is strictly larger. In the PID $\mathbb Z[i]$, $5 = (2 + i)(2 - i)$, and $2 - i$ is a Gaussian prime (norm $5$) that is not an associate of $2 + i$ (the associates of $2 + i$ are $\pm(2 + i)$, $\pm(1 - 2i)$; see [[gaussian-integers]]). By unique factorisation no power $(2 + i)^n$ is divisible by $2 - i$, so the prime $(2 - i)$ is disjoint from $\{(2 + i)^n\}$ and extends to a proper prime of $R$ containing $5$. Thus $1/5 \notin R$, and $R$ is not the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/5]$; it does not even contain $\mathbb Z[1/5]$.

In general let $\beta = N(\alpha)/\alpha$, the product of the conjugates of $\alpha$ other than $\alpha$ itself. It lies in $K$ and is an algebraic integer, so $\beta \in \mathcal O_K$, and $1/\alpha = \beta/N(\alpha)$. Hence always $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha] \subseteq \mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)]$, and the latter is the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/N(\alpha)]$. Equality holds iff $N(\alpha)$ is a unit of $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$, i.e. (by the description of the units of $D[1/\alpha]$ as the elements outside every prime not containing $\alpha$, [[localization]]) iff every prime of $\mathcal O_K$ containing $N(\alpha)$ contains $\alpha$. This holds when $\alpha \in \mathbb Z$, since then $N(\alpha) = \alpha^{[K:\mathbb Q]}$, which covers their rings $\mathcal O_K[1/n]$ (Theorem 4.5); it fails for $\alpha = 2 + i$ at the prime $(2 - i)$. Their proof of Theorem 4.2 correctly shows that $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ is integrally closed and that $1/\alpha$ is integral over $\mathbb Z[1/N(\alpha)]$; what is missing, and false here, is that $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha]$ contains $1/N(\alpha)$. Their Corollary 4.4 applies Theorem 4.1 to $N(\alpha)$ directly and does not depend on Theorem 4.2: for Galois $K$, $(N(\alpha)) = \prod_\sigma\sigma((\alpha))$, so the primes dividing $N(\alpha)$ are the Galois conjugates of those dividing $\alpha$, and $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)])$ is $\operatorname{Cl}_K$ modulo the subgroup generated by the conjugates of their classes.

blocks.title: Conjugation and localisation
blocks.body: Coykendall and Kettinger (Example 5.1, Theorem 5.8) ask when a Galois automorphism $\sigma$ preserves an overring of $\mathcal O_K$. Let $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, $\sigma$ complex conjugation and $\alpha = 1 + \sqrt{-5}$. Show that $\sigma(D_{\mathfrak p}) = D_{\sigma(\mathfrak p)}$ for every prime $\mathfrak p$, but that $R = D[1/\alpha]$ satisfies $\sigma(R) \ne R$.
blocks.solution:
$\sigma$ is a ring automorphism of $D$, extended to $K$ by $\sigma(a/s) = \sigma(a)/\sigma(s)$. It maps $D \setminus \mathfrak p$ bijectively onto $D \setminus \sigma(\mathfrak p)$, so $\sigma(D_{\mathfrak p}) = D_{\sigma(\mathfrak p)}$. Likewise $\sigma(R) = D[1/\sigma(\alpha)] = D[1/(1 - \sqrt{-5})]$.

So $\sigma(R) \subseteq R$ would require $1 - \sqrt{-5}$ to be a unit of $R$, i.e. to lie in no prime of $D$ disjoint from $\{\alpha^n\}$. Consider $\chi\colon D 	o \mathbb F_3$, $a + b\sqrt{-5} \mapsto a + b  mod 3$, a ring map because $(\sqrt{-5})^2 = -5 \equiv 1 = 1^2 \pmod 3$. Its kernel contains $3$ and $1 - \sqrt{-5}$, and $a + b\sqrt{-5} = (a + b) - b(1 - \sqrt{-5})$ shows the kernel is $(3, 1 - \sqrt{-5}) = P_3'$. Since $\chi(\alpha) = 2 
e 0$, $P_3'$ contains no power of $\alpha$, so $P_3'R$ is a proper prime of $R$ containing $1 - \sqrt{-5}$. Hence $1/(1 - \sqrt{-5}) = \sigma(1/\alpha) 
otin R$ and $\sigma(R) 
e R$. This is the paper's observation that $	frac1\alpha\,\sigma(	frac1\alpha) = 	frac16 
otin R$ (indeed $6 \in P_3'$). In the language of their Theorem 5.8: $P_3 = \sigma(P_3') = (3, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$ satisfies $P_3R = R$ since it contains $\alpha$, while $\sigma(P_3)R = P_3'R 
e R$.

items.q: Show that $\mathbb Z[i][1/(1+i)] = \mathbb Z[i][1/2]$.
items.solution: Since $2 = -i(1 + i)^2$, $1/2 = i/(1 + i)^2 \in \mathbb Z[i][1/(1+i)]$; and $1/(1 + i) = (1 - i)/2 \in \mathbb Z[i][1/2]$. So each ring contains the generators of the other. In the language of the norm example: $N(1 + i) = 2$, and the only prime containing $2$ is $(1 + i)$, which contains $1 + i$, so here inverting $\alpha$ and inverting $N(\alpha)$ agree.

items.q: Compute $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}][1/3])$ and $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}][1/7])$.
items.hint: Which primes divide $(3)$ and $(7)$, and what are their classes?
items.solution: $(3) = P_3P_3'$ and $(7) = P_7P_7'$, and all four primes are non-principal, so their classes equal $[P_2]$, the generator of $\operatorname{Cl}(D) \cong \mathbb Z/2$. Quotienting by the subgroup they generate leaves the trivial group in both cases: $D[1/3]$ and $D[1/7]$ are PIDs. (Inverting $11$, which stays prime in $D$ since $-5$ is not a square modulo $11$, would not change the class group: $(11)$ is principal.)

items.q: Let $K$ be a number field and $0 \ne n \in \mathbb Z$. Show that $\mathcal O_K[1/n]$ is the integral closure of $\mathbb Z[1/n]$ in $K$ and that $\sigma(\mathcal O_K[1/n]) = \mathcal O_K[1/n]$ for every automorphism $\sigma$ of $K$.
items.hint: Integral closure commutes with localisation; $\sigma(n) = n$.
items.solution: By [[localization]] (integral closure commutes with localisation, applied to $\mathbb Z \to K$ and $S = \{n^k\}$), the integral closure of $S^{-1}\mathbb Z = \mathbb Z[1/n]$ in $S^{-1}K = K$ is $S^{-1}\mathcal O_K = \mathcal O_K[1/n]$. An automorphism $\sigma$ maps $\mathcal O_K$ onto itself (it preserves monic integer equations) and fixes $n$, so $\sigma(a/n^k) = \sigma(a)/n^k$ and $\sigma(\mathcal O_K[1/n]) = \mathcal O_K[1/n]$.

items.q: Let $D$ be a Dedekind domain with finite class group. Show that there is $\alpha \in D$ with $D[1/\alpha]$ a PID.
items.hint: Choose integral ideals representing all classes and an element in their product.
items.solution: Let $J_1, \dots, J_h$ be integral ideals representing the $h$ classes (multiply any representative by a common denominator). Pick $0 \ne \alpha \in J_1\cdots J_h$. Then each $J_i$ divides $(\alpha)$, so every prime factor of every $J_i$ divides $(\alpha)$, and $[J_i]$ lies in the subgroup generated by the classes of the primes dividing $(\alpha)$. That subgroup is therefore all of $\operatorname{Cl}(D)$, and by the theorem $\operatorname{Cl}(D[1/\alpha]) = 1$. (If $h = 1$ take $\alpha = 1$.)

items.q: In $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, list the primes $\mathfrak p$ with $\mathfrak pD[1/6] = D[1/6]$, and show $D[1/6] = \bigcap D_{\mathfrak p}$ over the remaining nonzero primes.
items.solution: The primes meeting $\{6^n\}$ are those containing $6$, i.e. dividing $(6) = P_2^2P_3P_3'$: $P_2, P_3, P_3'$. By the intersection theorem $D[1/6] = \bigcap D_{\mathfrak p}$ over the primes avoiding $\{6^n\}$, which are $(0)$ and the nonzero primes other than $P_2, P_3, P_3'$; the factor $D_{(0)} = K$ can be dropped (there are other primes, so the intersection is unchanged).

items.q: With $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, $\alpha = 1 + \sqrt{-5}$ and $\sigma$ complex conjugation, show that $D[1/\alpha] \cap D[1/\sigma(\alpha)] = D[1/2]$.
items.hint: Write each ring as an intersection of local rings using $(\alpha) = P_2P_3$ and $(\sigma(\alpha)) = P_2P_3'$.
items.solution:
By the intersection theorem, $D[1/\alpha] =  igcap_{\mathfrak p 
e P_2, P_3} D_{\mathfrak p}$ and $D[1/\sigma(\alpha)] =  igcap_{\mathfrak p 
e P_2, P_3'} D_{\mathfrak p}$ (over nonzero primes; the primes containing $\alpha$ are $P_2, P_3$, those containing $\sigma(\alpha)$ are $P_2, P_3'$). Their intersection is the intersection of $D_{\mathfrak p}$ over the union of the two index sets, all nonzero primes except $P_2$ (since $P_3 
e P_3'$). The only prime containing $2$ is $P_2$ ($(2) = P_2^2$), so this is $D[1/2]$, again by the intersection theorem. In particular the intersection of the two overrings is strictly bigger than $D$.

items.q: Show that every ring $R$ with $\mathbb Z \subseteq R \subseteq \mathbb Q$ equals $\mathbb Z[1/p : p \in P]$ for a set $P$ of primes, and is the intersection of the $\mathbb Z_{(q)}$ for $q \notin P$. (This is Gilmer's statement in the simplest case.)
items.hint: If $a/b \in R$ in lowest terms, show $1/b \in R$.
items.solution: Let $P$ be the set of primes $p$ with $1/p \in R$. If $a/b \in R$ in lowest terms, write $ua + vb = 1$; then $1/b = u(a/b) + v \in R$, and $1/p = (b/p)(1/b) \in R$ for each prime $p \mid b$, so $p \in P$. Hence $R \subseteq \mathbb Z[1/p : p \in P]$, and the reverse inclusion holds by definition of $P$. This ring is $S^{-1}\mathbb Z$ with $S$ the products of primes in $P$; the primes of $\mathbb Z$ avoiding $S$ are $(0)$ and the $(q)$ with $q \notin P$, so by the intersection theorem $R = \bigcap_{q \notin P}\mathbb Z_{(q)}$ (when $P$ contains all primes, $R = \mathbb Q$ is the empty intersection inside $\mathbb Q$).

blocks.body:
- $S^{-1}D$ is Dedekind, and $\operatorname{Cl}(S^{-1}D) = \operatorname{Cl}(D)/\langle[\mathfrak p] : \mathfrak p \cap S \ne \varnothing\rangle$; for $D[1/\alpha]$ kill the classes of the primes dividing $\alpha$.
- $S^{-1}D = \bigcap_{\mathfrak p \cap S = \varnothing} D_{\mathfrak p}$; Gilmer: every overring of $D$ is such an intersection.
- $\mathcal O_K[1/\alpha] \subseteq \mathcal O_K[1/N(\alpha)]$, with equality iff every prime containing $N(\alpha)$ contains $\alpha$ (e.g. $\alpha \in \mathbb Z$); $\mathbb Z[i][1/(2 + i)]$ is a counterexample to equality.
- Inverting finitely many elements can make any Dedekind domain with finite class group a PID.

blocks.title: Rings of integers and integral closures
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to prove that the ring of integers of a number field, and more generally the integral closure of a Dedekind domain in a finite separable extension, is a Dedekind domain, and you will know the vocabulary of primes lying over a prime.

Why: every example of a Dedekind domain on this page that is not a PID, such as $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, was used on the strength of the claim that rings of integers are Dedekind. Integral closedness is built into the definition of $\mathcal O_K$; the work is to show Noetherianity and dimension $\le 1$. We follow Sutherland's treatment of Dedekind extensions (Lecture 4, §4.5, the "AKLB" setup); Baanen et al. formalise the same proof (§7), and Gathmann gives a shorter argument for $\mathbb Z$ (Proposition 13.5).

Setup (AKLB): $A$ is a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$, $L/K$ a finite separable field extension of degree $n$, and $B$ the integral closure of $A$ in $L$ (the elements of $L$ that are roots of monic polynomials over $A$). We use from [[fields-ext]] and [[galois]] the trace $T_{L/K}(x)$ and norm $N_{L/K}(x)$ (trace and determinant of multiplication by $x$), the fact that integral elements form a ring and that integrality is transitive, and, for separable $L/K$, that the trace form $(x, y) \mapsto T_{L/K}(xy)$ is nondegenerate (Sutherland, Proposition 4.58; not reproved here).

blocks.title: Three lemmas
blocks.body:
In the AKLB setup:

1. Every $x \in L$ can be written $x = b/a$ with $b \in B$ and $0 \ne a \in A$. In particular $\operatorname{Frac} B = L$, and $B$ contains a $K$-basis of $L$.
2. If $b \in B$, then $T_{L/K}(b) \in A$ and $N_{L/K}(b) \in A$.
3. If $A \subseteq B$ is any integral extension of rings and $\mathfrak q_0 \subsetneq \mathfrak q_1$ are primes of $B$, then $\mathfrak q_0 \cap A \subsetneq \mathfrak q_1 \cap A$. Hence $\dim B \le \dim A$.

1. (Sutherland, Proposition 4.55.) $x$ is algebraic over $K$; clearing denominators, $a_mx^m + a_{m-1}x^{m-1} + \dots + a_0 = 0$ with $a_i \in A$, $a_m \ne 0$. Multiply by $a_m^{m-1}$:
$$(a_mx)^m + a_{m-1}(a_mx)^{m-1} + a_{m-2}a_m(a_mx)^{m-2} + \dots + a_0a_m^{m-1} = 0,$$
a monic equation for $a_mx$ over $A$. So $b = a_mx \in B$ and $x = b/a_m$. Applying this to a $K$-basis of $L$ and clearing denominators gives a basis inside $B$.

2. (Sutherland, Proposition 4.56.) Let $f$ be the minimal polynomial of $b$ over $K$. In a splitting field, each root of $f$ is a conjugate of $b$ and satisfies the same monic equation over $A$ as $b$, so it is integral over $A$; the coefficients of $f$ are sums of products of roots, hence integral over $A$, and they lie in $K$, so they lie in $A$ because $A$ is integrally closed. If $f = x^d + c_{d-1}x^{d-1} + \dots + c_0$ and $m = [L : K(b)]$, then $T_{L/K}(b) = -m\,c_{d-1}$ and $N_{L/K}(b) = \bigl((-1)^dc_0\bigr)^m$; so both lie in $A$.

3. (Sutherland, Lemma 4.62.) Replace $A \subseteq B$ by $\bar A = A/(\mathfrak q_0 \cap A) \subseteq \bar B = B/\mathfrak q_0$, still integral, with $\bar B$ a domain. Pick $0 \ne x \in \mathfrak q_1/\mathfrak q_0$ and a monic equation $x^m + c_{m-1}x^{m-1} + \dots + c_0 = 0$ over $\bar A$ of least degree. Then $c_0 \ne 0$ (otherwise divide by $x$, possible in the domain $\bar B$, and lower the degree), and $c_0 = -x(x^{m-1} + \dots + c_1) \in \mathfrak q_1/\mathfrak q_0$. So $c_0$ is a nonzero element of $(\mathfrak q_1 \cap A)/(\mathfrak q_0 \cap A)$. A chain of primes of length $d$ in $B$ thus contracts to a chain of length $d$ in $A$.

blocks.title: Integral closures of Dedekind domains are Dedekind
blocks.body: In the AKLB setup, $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-module and a Dedekind domain. In particular, for every number field $K$ the ring of integers $\mathcal O_K$ (the integral closure of $\mathbb Z$ in $K$) is a Dedekind domain and a free abelian group of rank $[K : \mathbb Q]$; and the integral closure of $\mathbb F_q[t]$ in a finite separable extension of $\mathbb F_q(t)$ is a Dedekind domain.

(Sutherland, Proposition 4.60 and Theorem 4.63.)

Integrally closed: an element of $L = \operatorname{Frac} B$ integral over $B$ is integral over $A$ by transitivity, so it lies in $B$.

Dimension: by Lemma 3, $\dim B \le \dim A \le 1$.

Finitely generated, hence Noetherian. By Lemma 1 choose a $K$-basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$ of $L$ inside $B$. As the trace form is nondegenerate, there is a dual basis $e_1', \dots, e_n'$ with $T_{L/K}(e_i'e_j) = \delta_{ij}$. Let $b \in B$ and write $b = \sum_i x_ie_i'$ with $x_i \in K$. Then
$$x_j = T_{L/K}(b\,e_j) \in A$$
by Lemma 2, since $be_j \in B$. Hence
$$B \subseteq Ae_1' + \dots + Ae_n',$$
a finitely generated $A$-module. Over the Noetherian ring $A$, a submodule of a finitely generated module is finitely generated, so $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-module. Every ideal of $B$ is an $A$-submodule of $B$, hence finitely generated over $A$ and a fortiori over $B$: $B$ is Noetherian.

For $A = \mathbb Z$: $\mathcal O_K$ is a subgroup of the free abelian group $\mathbb Ze_1' + \dots + \mathbb Ze_n'$ of rank $n$, hence free of rank at most $n$, and it contains the $n$ linearly independent elements $e_1, \dots, e_n$; so it is free of rank $n = [K : \mathbb Q]$. For $A = \mathbb F_q[t]$ the same argument applies.

- Separability is used only to get the dual basis. Without it, $B$ need not be finitely generated over $A$ (Sutherland, Remark 4.61), but $B$ is still a Dedekind domain by the Krull-Akizuki theorem (Remark 4.64; the Stacks Project, Lemma 10.120.18, proves it for any Noetherian domain $A$ of dimension $1$).
- The extension must be finite. The integral closure of $\mathbb Z$ in the algebraic closure of $\mathbb Q$ is not Noetherian (the chain of square roots of $2$ in the examples), so not Dedekind.
- $B$ is a finitely generated torsion-free $A$-module, but need not be free over $A$ when $A$ is not a PID; it is free iff its Steinitz class is trivial (last section). Being generated by one element as a ring, $B = A[\theta]$ ("monogenic"), is stronger still and often fails; the index $[\mathcal O_K : \mathbb Z[\theta]]$ is the subject of papers such as Jakhar-Kaur-Kumar.

blocks.title: The trace form bound for Q(√5)
blocks.body: Let $K = \mathbb Q(\sqrt 5)$. Use the dual basis argument with $e_1 = 1$, $e_2 = \sqrt 5$ to find a lattice containing $\mathcal O_K$, and then determine $\mathcal O_K$.
blocks.solution:
Traces: $T(1) = 2$, $T(\sqrt 5) = 0$, $T(5) = 10$ (the trace of $a + b\sqrt 5$ is $2a$). The matrix $\bigl(T(e_ie_j)\bigr)$ is $\mathrm{diag}(2, 10)$, so the dual basis is $e_1' = \tfrac12$, $e_2' = \tfrac{\sqrt 5}{10}$ (check: $T(\tfrac12\cdot 1) = 1$, $T(\tfrac{\sqrt5}{10}\sqrt5) = T(\tfrac12) = 1$, and the mixed traces vanish). Hence
$$\mathcal O_K \subseteq \mathbb Z\cdot\tfrac12 + \mathbb Z\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt 5}{10}.$$
Now test $x = \tfrac a2 + \tfrac{b\sqrt5}{10}$ with $a, b \in \mathbb Z$. It is integral iff its trace $a$ and norm
$$\frac{a^2}{4} - \frac{5b^2}{100} = \frac{5a^2 - b^2}{20}$$
are integers. So $b^2 \equiv 5a^2 \pmod{20}$; modulo $5$ this forces $5 \mid b$, say $b = 5c$, and then $25c^2 \equiv 5a^2 \pmod{20}$, i.e. $5c^2 \equiv a^2 \pmod 4$, i.e. $c \equiv a \pmod 2$. So $x = \tfrac{a + c\sqrt 5}{2}$ with $a \equiv c \pmod 2$, and
$$\mathcal O_K = \Bigl\{\tfrac{a + c\sqrt5}{2} : a \equiv c \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2)\Bigr\} = \mathbb Z\Bigl[\tfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{2}\Bigr],$$
in agreement with the formula on [[ideals]]. The dual lattice is $10$ times larger in area than $\mathbb Z[\sqrt 5]$; it bounds $\mathcal O_K$, which turns out to have index $2$ over $\mathbb Z[\sqrt 5]$.

blocks.title: Primes lying over a prime
blocks.body:
In the AKLB setup let $\mathfrak p$ be a nonzero prime of $A$. Then $\mathfrak pB \ne B$, and in the Dedekind domain $B$
$$\mathfrak pB = \mathfrak q_1^{e_1}\cdots\mathfrak q_g^{e_g}$$
with distinct primes $\mathfrak q_i$. These are exactly the primes $\mathfrak q$ of $B$ with $\mathfrak q \cap A = \mathfrak p$, the primes lying over $\mathfrak p$, written $\mathfrak q \mid \mathfrak p$. The exponent $e_i$ is the ramification index and $f_i = [B/\mathfrak q_i : A/\mathfrak p]$ the residue degree. One says $\mathfrak p$ ramifies if some $e_i > 1$ (or a residue field extension is inseparable), splits completely if $g = n$, and is inert if $\mathfrak pB$ is prime. The fundamental identity $\sum_i e_if_i = n$ and its refinements are the subject of the separate page on splitting of primes; see Sutherland's Lecture 5.

Why $\mathfrak pB \ne B$ and why the $\mathfrak q_i$ are the primes over $\mathfrak p$: localise at $\mathfrak p$. $B_{\mathfrak p} = (A \setminus \mathfrak p)^{-1}B$ is a finitely generated module over the local ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$ (as $B$ is finitely generated over $A$), and it is nonzero. If $\mathfrak pB = B$, then $(\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p})B_{\mathfrak p} = B_{\mathfrak p}$, and Nakayama's lemma ([[local-rings]]) gives $B_{\mathfrak p} = 0$, a contradiction. For a prime $\mathfrak q$ of $B$: if $\mathfrak q \supseteq \mathfrak pB$, then $\mathfrak q \cap A$ is a prime containing the maximal ideal $\mathfrak p$ and not containing $1$, so it equals $\mathfrak p$; conversely $\mathfrak q \cap A = \mathfrak p$ gives $\mathfrak q \supseteq \mathfrak pB$. By contain-equals-divide, the primes containing $\mathfrak pB$ are those in its factorisation.

rows.text: 'Prime' usually means nonzero prime; $\mathfrak q \mid \mathfrak p$ ('$\mathfrak q$ lies over $\mathfrak p$') means $\mathfrak q \supseteq \mathfrak pB$, equivalently $\mathfrak q \cap A = \mathfrak p$; $\mathfrak q$ is unramified if $e_{\mathfrak q} = 1$ and $B/\mathfrak q$ is separable over $A/\mathfrak p$. He writes $B_{\mathfrak p}$ for the localisation of $B$ at the multiplicative set $A \setminus \mathfrak p$, not at a prime of $B$.

For $K/\mathbb Q$ one writes $p\mathcal O_K = \prod\mathfrak P_i^{e_i}$ with residue degrees $f_i$ (Jakhar-Kaur-Kumar §3), and $g$ for the number of primes; 'totally ramified' means a single prime with $e = n$.

blocks.title: Primes over 2, 3, 5 and 13 in the Gaussian integers
blocks.body: In $\mathbb Z[i]$, the integral closure of $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q(i)$, find the factorisations of $2\mathbb Z[i]$, $3\mathbb Z[i]$, $5\mathbb Z[i]$ and $13\mathbb Z[i]$, with $e$, $f$, $g$, and check $\sum e_if_i = 2$ in each case.
blocks.solution:
From [[gaussian-integers]]: $2 = -i(1 + i)^2$, so $2\mathbb Z[i] = (1 + i)^2$, with $e = 2$, $f = 1$ ($\mathbb Z[i]/(1 + i) \cong \mathbb F_2$, as $N(1 + i) = 2$), $g = 1$: $2$ ramifies, $2\cdot 1 = 2$.

$3$ is a Gaussian prime ($3 \equiv 3 \pmod 4$), and $\mathbb Z[i]/(3) \cong \mathbb F_3[x]/(x^2 + 1) \cong \mathbb F_9$: $e = 1$, $f = 2$, $g = 1$; $3$ is inert, $1 \cdot 2 = 2$.

$5 = (2 + i)(2 - i)$ and $13 = (3 + 2i)(3 - 2i)$ with non-associate factors of norm $5$, resp. $13$: $e = f = 1$, $g = 2$; these primes split completely, $1 + 1 = 2$.

In each case the norms confirm the residue degrees: a prime $\mathfrak q$ over $p$ has $N(\mathfrak q) = |\mathbb Z[i]/\mathfrak q| = p^f$.

items.q: Why is $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ the full ring of integers of $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5})$, and hence Dedekind?
items.a: Because $-5 \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, so the formula for quadratic rings of integers on [[ideals]] gives $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$; rings of integers are Dedekind by the theorem.

items.q: Where in the proof is separability used?
items.a: Only to have a dual basis for the trace form, which bounds $B$ inside a finitely generated $A$-module.

items.q: In $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, what are $e$, $f$, $g$ for $p = 2$ and $p = 3$?
Show that the integral closure of $\mathbb Z$ in $\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-5})$ is $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$.
items.hint: $x = u + v\sqrt{-5}$ ($u, v \in \mathbb Q$) is integral iff its trace $2u$ and norm $u^2 + 5v^2$ are integers.
items.solution: If $x$ is integral then $2u \in \mathbb Z$ and $u^2 + 5v^2 \in \mathbb Z$ (Lemma 2; conversely these make $x$ a root of the monic integer polynomial $X^2 - 2uX + u^2 + 5v^2$). Then $4u^2 + 20v^2 \in 4\mathbb Z$ and $(2u)^2 \in \mathbb Z$, so $20v^2 \in \mathbb Z$, so $2v \in \mathbb Z$ (if $v = r/s$ in lowest terms, $s^2 \mid 20r^2$ forces $s \mid 2$). Put $a = 2u$, $b = 2v$: $a^2 + 5b^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4$. Squares are $0$ or $1$ modulo $4$ and $5b^2 \equiv b^2$, so $a^2 + b^2 \equiv 0 \pmod 4$ forces $a, b$ even. So $u, v \in \mathbb Z$.

items.q: Factor $7\mathbb Z[i]$ and $29\mathbb Z[i]$, and give $e, f, g$.
items.hint: $7 \equiv 3$ and $29 \equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
items.solution: $-1$ is not a square mod $7$, so $x^2 + 1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb F_7$ and $7$ is inert: $e = 1$, $f = 2$, $g = 1$. $29 = 5^2 + 2^2 = (5 + 2i)(5 - 2i)$, two non-associate primes of norm $29$: $e = f = 1$, $g = 2$.

items.q: Let $L = K(\sqrt d)$ be a quadratic extension of $K = \operatorname{Frac} A$ ($\operatorname{char} K \ne 2$, $d \in A$ not a square in $K$). Prove Lemma 2 directly: if $b = x + y\sqrt d$ ($x, y \in K$) is integral over $A$ then $2x \in A$ and $x^2 - dy^2 \in A$.
items.hint: The conjugate $x - y\sqrt d$ satisfies the same monic equation.
items.solution: The automorphism $\sqrt d \mapsto -\sqrt d$ of $L/K$ maps a monic equation over $A$ satisfied by $b$ to the same equation, so $\bar b = x - y\sqrt d$ is integral over $A$. Integral elements form a ring, so $b + \bar b = 2x$ and $b\bar b = x^2 - dy^2$ are integral over $A$; they lie in $K$, and $A$ is integrally closed, so they lie in $A$. These are $T_{L/K}(b)$ and $N_{L/K}(b)$.

items.q: In the AKLB setup with $A$ having finite residue fields, show that $B$ has finite residue fields, and that for $\mathfrak q \mid \mathfrak p$, $N(\mathfrak q) = N(\mathfrak p)^{f}$ where $f$ is the residue degree.
items.hint: $B/\mathfrak pB$ is a finitely generated module over the field $A/\mathfrak p$.
items.solution: $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-module, say by $n'$ elements, so $B/\mathfrak pB$ is spanned by $n'$ elements over $A/\mathfrak p$ and is finite. For $\mathfrak q \mid \mathfrak p$, $B/\mathfrak q$ is a quotient of $B/\mathfrak pB$, hence finite, and it is a field extension of $A/\mathfrak p$ of degree $f$, so $|B/\mathfrak q| = |A/\mathfrak p|^f$.

items.q: Prove that $\mathcal O_K$ is Noetherian by Gathmann's route, without the trace form: show that $\mathcal O_K/p\mathcal O_K$ is finite for every prime $p$, deduce that $\mathcal O_K/m\mathcal O_K$ is finite for every $m \ge 1$, and that every nonzero ideal contains a nonzero integer.
items.hint: Elements of $\mathcal O_K$ that are linearly independent over $\mathbb Z$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$; for an ideal $I \ne 0$ take $0 \ne x \in I$ and look at the constant term of its minimal polynomial.
items.solution: (a) If $\bar x_1, \dots, \bar x_r \in \mathcal O_K/p\mathcal O_K$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb F_p$, then $x_1, \dots, x_r$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$: a relation $\sum q_ix_i = 0$ can be scaled to integers $c_i$ not all divisible by $p$, and reducing mod $p$ gives a nontrivial relation among the $\bar x_i$. So $\dim_{\mathbb F_p}\mathcal O_K/p\mathcal O_K \le [K:\mathbb Q]$, and the quotient is finite. (b) For $m = m_1m_2$ the exact sequence $$0 \to \frac{m_1\mathcal O_K}{m\mathcal O_K} \to \frac{\mathcal O_K}{m\mathcal O_K} \to \frac{\mathcal O_K}{m_1\mathcal O_K} \to 0$$ and $m_1\mathcal O_K/m_1m_2\mathcal O_K \cong \mathcal O_K/m_2\mathcal O_K$ (multiplication by $m_1$, injective in a domain) give finiteness by induction on the number of prime factors. (c) If $0 \ne x \in I$ has minimal polynomial $X^k + c_{k-1}X^{k-1} + \dots + c_0$ over $\mathbb Q$ with $c_i \in \mathbb Z$ (Lemma 2's argument) and $c_0 \ne 0$, then $c_0 = -x(x^{k-1} + \dots + c_1) \in I \cap \mathbb Z$. So $I \supseteq m\mathcal O_K$ with $m = |c_0|$, and $I/m\mathcal O_K$ is finite; $I$ is generated by $m$ and finitely many representatives. Hence every ideal is finitely generated. (Gathmann's proof of (c) uses dimension theory; the constant term argument is the one in Lemma 3.)

blocks.body:
- AKLB: the integral closure $B$ of a Dedekind domain $A$ in a finite separable $L/K$ is Dedekind and a finitely generated $A$-module; rings of integers are Dedekind and free of rank $[K:\mathbb Q]$ over $\mathbb Z$.
- Ingredients: $L = \operatorname{Frac} B$; traces of integral elements lie in $A$; integral extensions do not increase dimension; the dual basis of the trace form bounds $B$.
- Without separability the theorem still holds (Krull-Akizuki), but $B$ may not be finite over $A$.
- $\mathfrak pB = \prod\mathfrak q_i^{e_i}$ over the primes lying over $\mathfrak p$, with ramification indices $e_i$ and residue degrees $f_i$; their theory is a separate page.

blocks.title: Modules over a Dedekind domain
blocks.body:
After this section you will be able to classify finitely generated modules over a Dedekind domain, compute the Steinitz class of a torsion-free module, and explain why $\mathcal O_L$ need not be free over $\mathcal O_K$.

Why: over a PID every finitely generated torsion-free module is free. Over $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ the ideal $P_2$ is torsion-free of rank $1$ but not free (a free module of rank $1$ is $D x \cong D$, i.e. a principal ideal). Yet, as we will see, $P_2 \oplus P_2 \cong D^2$ is free. The class group is exactly what is left of freeness. We follow the University of Washington Math 505 notes 'Lecture 2-26' for the proofs, and Gargava et al. for the Steinitz class as it appears in papers; Wikipedia attributes the results to Steinitz (1912).

blocks.title: Ideals as modules
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain with fraction field $K$, and $I, J$ nonzero fractional ideals.

1. $I \cong J$ as $A$-modules iff $[I] = [J]$ in $\operatorname{Cl}(A)$.
2. $I \oplus J \cong A \oplus IJ$.
3. Every nonzero fractional ideal is a projective $A$-module, and $I_1 \oplus \dots \oplus I_n \cong A^{n-1} \oplus I_1\cdots I_n$.

1. If $J = xI$, multiplication by $x$ is an isomorphism. Conversely let $\varphi\colon I \to J$ be an isomorphism and $x, y \in I$ nonzero. Write $y/x = r/s$ with $r, s \in A$; then $sy = rx$, so $s\varphi(y) = \varphi(sy) = \varphi(rx) = r\varphi(x)$, i.e. $\varphi(y)/y = \varphi(x)/x$. So $\varphi$ is multiplication by a fixed $k \in K^\times$ and $J = kI$.

2. Neither side changes, up to isomorphism, if $I$ is replaced by $cI$ ($c \in K^\times$), by part 1 applied to $I$ and to $IJ$. Scaling, we may assume $I$ and $J$ are integral; by the theorem on moving ideals, in the form of the exercise after it (every class contains an integral ideal coprime to a given ideal), we may also replace $I$ by an integral ideal in its class coprime to $J$, so $I + J = A$. Then $\varphi\colon I \oplus J \to A$, $(i, j) \mapsto i + j$, is surjective with kernel $\{(x, -x) : x \in I \cap J\} \cong I \cap J = IJ$ (coprime ideals). Since $A$ is free, the exact sequence $0 \to IJ \to I \oplus J \to A \to 0$ splits, and $I \oplus J \cong A \oplus IJ$.

3. $I \oplus I^{-1} \cong A \oplus A$, so $I$ is a direct summand of a free module, i.e. projective. The formula follows from part 2 by induction: $I_1 \oplus I_2 \oplus \cdots \cong A \oplus I_1I_2 \oplus I_3 \oplus \cdots$.

blocks.title: Structure of finitely generated modules
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be a Dedekind domain and $M$ a finitely generated $A$-module, with torsion submodule $T$.

1. $M \cong T \oplus M/T$, and $M/T$ is projective.
2. A finitely generated torsion-free module $N$ of rank $n \ge 1$ (i.e. $\dim_K N \otimes_A K = n$) is isomorphic to $A^{n-1} \oplus I$ for a nonzero ideal $I$, and $A^{n-1} \oplus I \cong A^{n-1} \oplus J$ iff $[I] = [J]$. The class $[I] \in \operatorname{Cl}(A)$ is the Steinitz class of $N$. In particular a finitely generated module is projective iff it is torsion-free.
3. $T \cong \bigoplus_i A/\mathfrak p_i^{n_i}$ for finitely many primes $\mathfrak p_i$ (not necessarily distinct) and exponents $n_i \ge 1$, uniquely up to order.

We prove the existence part of 2, and 1; uniqueness in 2 is proved in the last exercise below, and 3 and the uniqueness in 3 are in the Math 505 notes (Theorem 22), where they are derived from the Chinese remainder theorem much as for PIDs.

2 (existence). $N$ embeds in $N \otimes_A K \cong K^n$ because it is torsion-free (the kernel of $N \to N \otimes K = S^{-1}N$, $S = A \setminus 0$, is the torsion, [[localization]]). Induct on $n$. Let $\pi\colon N \to K$ be the last coordinate. Its image is a finitely generated nonzero $A$-submodule of $K$ (if it were zero, $N$ would lie in $K^{n-1}$, contradicting rank $n$), i.e. a fractional ideal, hence projective; so $N \cong \ker\pi \oplus \pi(N)$. The kernel is a submodule of the Noetherian module $N$, hence finitely generated, torsion-free, of rank $n - 1$. By induction $N$ is a direct sum of $n$ nonzero fractional ideals, and by the previous theorem it is $\cong A^{n-1} \oplus I$; multiplying $I$ by a common denominator we may take $I$ integral.

1. $M/T$ is finitely generated and torsion-free, hence projective by 2, so $M \to M/T$ splits.

blocks.title: A non-free ideal whose square-sum is free
blocks.body: In $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ show that $P_2 \oplus P_2 \cong D \oplus D$ by following the proof of part 2 of the theorem on ideals as modules.
blocks.solution:
We need an ideal in the class of $P_2$ that is coprime to $P_2$. Since $P_2P_3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})$ and $P_2^2 = (2)$,
$$P_3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})P_2^{-1} = \tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-5}}{2}\,P_2,$$
so $P_3 \cong P_2$ as $D$-modules, and $P_3 + P_2 = D$ (distinct maximal ideals). Then
$$P_2 \oplus P_2 \cong P_3 \oplus P_2 \cong D \oplus P_2P_3 = D \oplus (1 + \sqrt{-5}) \cong D \oplus D,$$
the last step because a principal ideal $(\alpha) = D\alpha$ is free of rank $1$. Explicitly, $P_3 \oplus P_2 \to D$, $(x, y) \mapsto x + y$, is onto with kernel $\{(z, -z) : z \in P_2 \cap P_3\} \cong (1 + \sqrt{-5})$. The Steinitz class of $P_2 \oplus P_2$ is $[P_2]^2 = 1$; that of $D \oplus P_2$ is $[P_2] \ne 1$, so $D \oplus P_2$ is not free.

items.label: Last summand
items.body: Write a torsion-free module of rank $n$ as $A^{n-1} \oplus I$; the class $[I]$ is well defined and, with the rank, determines the module (Math 505 notes, Proposition 21; Gargava et al., Proposition 9; Wikipedia).

items.label: Determinants
items.body: Gargava et al. (Definition 7) define it for a module $M \subseteq K^t$ of rank $t$ as the class of the fractional ideal generated by all determinants $\det(v_1, \dots, v_t)$, $v_i \in M$; changing $M$ by an element of $\mathrm{GL}_t(K)$ multiplies all these determinants by one scalar, so the class does not change (their Remark 8). For $M = A^{t-1} \oplus I$ the determinant ideal is $I$.

items.label: Product of the ideals
items.body: If $M \cong I_1 \oplus \dots \oplus I_n$, the Steinitz class is $[I_1\cdots I_n]$; the Math 505 notes prove that $\bigoplus I_i \cong \bigoplus J_j$ iff the numbers of summands agree and $[I_1\cdots I_n] = [J_1\cdots J_m]$, by comparing determinants of the matrix of an isomorphism.

blocks.body:
- "Torsion-free" and "free" agree over a PID, not over a Dedekind domain: $P_2$ is torsion-free, projective and not free. A torsion-free module is free iff its Steinitz class is trivial.
- In particular, for an extension $L/K$ of number fields $\mathcal O_L$ is a projective $\mathcal O_K$-module of rank $[L:K]$, free iff its Steinitz class in $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathcal O_K)$ is trivial; if $\mathcal O_K$ is a PID it is always free.
- The decomposition $A^{n-1} \oplus I$ is not unique as a decomposition: only the rank and the class $[I]$ are invariants ($P_2 \oplus P_2 = D \oplus D$ up to isomorphism).

items.q: Is $P_3 \oplus P_7$ free over $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$?
items.a: Yes: its Steinitz class is $[P_3P_7] = [P_2]^2 = 1$; indeed $P_3P_7 = (1 - 2\sqrt{-5})$.

items.q: Is $D \oplus D \oplus P_3$ isomorphic to $D \oplus P_2 \oplus P_2 \oplus P_2$ over $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$?
items.a: No: the ranks are $3$ and $4$.

items.q: What is the Steinitz class of $D^2 \oplus P_2^{-1}$?
Show that a nonzero ideal $I$ of a Dedekind domain is a free $A$-module iff it is principal.
items.hint: A free module of rank $1$ is $A x$; what is the rank of $I$?
items.solution: $I \otimes_A K \cong IK = K$, so $I$ has rank $1$, and a free module of rank $1$ is $\cong A$. If $\varphi\colon A \to I$ is an isomorphism, then $I = A\varphi(1)$ is principal; conversely $(x) = Ax \cong A$ for $x \ne 0$.

items.q: Over $\mathbb Z[i]$, decompose the torsion module $\mathbb Z[i]/(5)$ as in part 3 of the structure theorem.
items.hint: $(5) = (2 + i)(2 - i)$ with coprime factors.
items.solution: By the Chinese remainder theorem $\mathbb Z[i]/(5) \cong \mathbb Z[i]/(2 + i) \oplus \mathbb Z[i]/(2 - i)$, each factor a field with $5$ elements.

items.q: Show that $P_3 \oplus P_7 \cong D \oplus D$ over $D = \mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$, and that $D \oplus P_3 \not\cong D \oplus D$.
items.hint: $P_3$ and $P_7$ are coprime and $P_3P_7$ is principal.
items.solution: $P_3 + P_7 = D$ (distinct maximal ideals), so part 2 gives $$\begin{aligned}P_3 \oplus P_7 &\cong D \oplus P_3P_7\\ &= D \oplus (1 - 2\sqrt{-5}) \cong D^2,\end{aligned}$$ using $P_3P_7 = (1 - 2\sqrt{-5})$ from the class group section. $D \oplus P_3$ has Steinitz class $[P_3] = [P_2] \ne 1$, while $D \oplus D$ has the trivial class, so they are not isomorphic by the uniqueness statement.

items.q: Show that every submodule of a finitely generated projective module over a Dedekind domain is projective.
items.hint: Projective modules are submodules of free modules, hence torsion-free.
items.solution: A finitely generated projective module $P$ is a direct summand of some $A^m$, so it is torsion-free, and so is every submodule $Q \subseteq P$. $Q$ is finitely generated because $A$ is Noetherian and $P$ is finitely generated. By the structure theorem a finitely generated torsion-free module is projective. (Dedekind domains are 'hereditary'; Wikipedia lists this as a characterisation.)

items.q: Prove the uniqueness of the Steinitz class for rank $2$: if $A \oplus I \cong A \oplus J$ for nonzero fractional ideals, then $[I] = [J]$.
items.hint: Regard both modules inside $K^2$ and compare the ideals generated by $2 \times 2$ determinants of pairs of elements.
items.solution: For an $A$-submodule $M \subseteq K^2$ let $\delta(M)$ be the $A$-submodule of $K$ generated by $\det(v, w)$, $v, w \in M$. For $M = A \oplus I$: $\det((a, x), (b, y)) = ay - bx \in I$, and $\det((1, 0), (0, x)) = x$, so $\delta(A \oplus I) = I$. An isomorphism $\varphi\colon A \oplus I \to A \oplus J$ extends to a $K$-linear automorphism of $K^2 = (A \oplus I) \otimes K$, given by a matrix $g \in \mathrm{GL}_2(K)$, and $\det(gv, gw) = \det(g)\det(v, w)$. Hence $J = \delta(\varphi(A \oplus I)) = \det(g)\,I$, so $[I] = [J]$. (This is the determinant idea of Gargava et al., Definition 7, and of the Math 505 notes; the same argument works for any rank with $n \times n$ determinants.)

blocks.body:
- $I \cong J$ as modules iff $[I] = [J]$; $I \oplus J \cong A \oplus IJ$; nonzero fractional ideals are projective of rank $1$.
- Finitely generated torsion-free modules are $A^{n-1} \oplus I$, classified by rank and Steinitz class $[I]$; projective = torsion-free for finitely generated modules.
- Every finitely generated module is torsion $\oplus$ projective, and the torsion is $\bigoplus A/\mathfrak p_i^{n_i}$.
- $\mathcal O_L$ is free over $\mathcal O_K$ iff its Steinitz class is trivial.

Prerequisites used on this page: [[ideals]] (prime ideals and factorisations in $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$), [[localization]] and [[local-rings]] (local rings $A_{\mathfrak p}$, what localisation preserves, Nakayama's lemma), [[noetherian-rings]], [[ufds]], [[fields-ext]] (trace and norm).

- [[class-group]]: finiteness of the class group of a number field via Minkowski's bound, reduced binary quadratic forms, class number one.
- [[dedekind-zeta]] and [[class-number-formula]]: unique factorisation of ideals gives the Euler product $\zeta_K(s) = \prod_{\mathfrak p}(1 - N\mathfrak p^{-s})^{-1}$, and the residue at $s = 1$ involves the class number.
- [[class-field-theory]]: ray class groups and the narrow class group generalise $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathcal O_K)$; the Hilbert class field has Galois group $\operatorname{Cl}(\mathcal O_K)$; every class contains infinitely many primes. Koymans and Pagano's work on the negative Pell equation uses class groups and narrow class groups of quadratic fields in this way.
- Splitting of primes in extensions (a separate page, proposed): ramification indices and residue degrees, $\sum e_if_i = n$, the Dedekind-Kummer theorem (stated for $\mathcal O_K = \mathbb Z[\alpha]$ on [[ideals]]), discriminants, decomposition and inertia groups in [[galois]] extensions; see also [[cyclotomic]].
- [[p-adic-numbers]] and [[hensel]]: completing the DVR $A_{\mathfrak p}$ gives complete DVRs such as $\mathbb Z_p$.
- [[algebraic-varieties]], [[riemann-roch]], [[elliptic-curves]] and [[schemes]]: the spectrum of a Dedekind domain is a regular one-dimensional scheme, coordinate rings of smooth affine curves are Dedekind, and the class group is the Picard group of the curve.
- Factorisation theory (Chang-Geroldinger) and computational class groups (Elsenhans-Voight: factor bases, relations and the Smith normal form) build on the class group; neither is covered here.
